articles.title: 'The Ave for All' Transforms U District's Main Thoroughfare
articles.author: Ryan Packer
paras: Seeing a street festival take over University Way NE through the heart of the U District is a common sight throughout most of the year. But this past Saturday, the attraction wasn't food vendors or craftspeople – it was the street itself. Visitors to one of the city's most beloved shopping districts were treated to a fully pedestrianized street as part of " The Ave for All ", which continues this upcoming Saturday, October 17 for a second weekend.

An idea advanced by the placemaking group U District Advocates, The Ave for All gives pedestrians breathing room to enjoy a leisurely Saturday without being crammed onto University Way's narrow sidewalks. Tables and chairs turned the periphery of the street into a patio that wasn't tied to any specific businesses, prompting more folks to stick around and linger...but also grab a bite nearby.

Games, including a large chess board, provided activation and a pair of buskers livened the mood. It didn't hurt that storm clouds, spitting rain in the early afternoon, cleared away and left a beautiful autumn day.
For event organizer L. Harrison Jerome, the Ave for All is a glimpse of how a neighborhood like the University District can better use one of its biggest stretches of real estate – the street.

"In this neighborhood, you see how thin the sidewalks are. Now people actually have the ability to move out into the space, and they're actually filling it,"Jerome told The Urbanist. "They're doing chalk art, they're hanging out with each other, they're playing games, they're having off street dining. It's really, really nice weather today, and people are just enjoying the street in a different way than they had before."

As a broader city, Seattle is taking small steps toward creating more pedestrian-oriented spaces out of underutilized stretches of roadway, with the Seattle Department of Transportation's People Streets and Public Spaces program at the forefront of that work. Potential public plazas are being eyed in the Admiral District, Delridge, and on Upper Queen Anne, projects that will ultimately be demonstrations of the idea of creating a pedestrian plaza at the heart of every neighborhood.
But The Ave for All is presenting a bolder vision of how a street at the heart of a business district can truly transform.

U District Advocates has pointed out that they are not the first group to dream of a fully pedestrian-oriented Ave, with storied Seattle architect Victor Steinbrueck putting the idea forward in 1955. The idea got closest to becoming a reality in the early 1970s, with the University District Development Council established specifically to advance the idea.

"The plan basically calls for a pedestrian mall on University Way NE to run from NE 47th to NE 42nd streets," a February 1972 story in the Seattle Post-Intelligencer noted. At that time, outgoing UDDC Executive Vice President David Rowlands touted the proposal for a U District pedestrian mall as creating "what Ghirardelli Square is to San Francisco, what the French Quarter is to New Orleans and what George-town is to Washington, D.C."

The year before in 1971, UDDC surveyed participants at the U District Street Fair finding 90% general support for the idea of a pedestrian mall ( sound familiar? ). But the proposal fell apart when property owners on the Ave were required to provide their stamp of approval. An alternative proposal put forward by neighborhood real estate broker Don Kennedy included a pedestrian plaza in front of what is now the UW tower connected to a "tremendous" parking garage with shops on top. That idea never came to fruition either.

Everything old is new again. Earlier this summer, the U District Advocates had a false start after the City of Seattle declined to approve an initial request to open up the Ave in late May and early June , with a number of nearby business owners opposing the plan.

As the Seattle Times reported at the time, the push back was orchestrated by Lois Ko and Emily Scully, owners of Sweet Alchemy and Shultzy’s Bar & Grill respectively. But after other business owners in the neighborhood found they'd been added to a list of opponents of the event without their knowledge, a cloud of animus and uncertainty grew up around the entire project that threatened to sour the spirit of The Ave for All.

While that's not exactly ancient history at this point, it did seem to be put in the rearview mirror this weekend. For the autumn re-do, U District Advocates was asked to jump through a few more hoops to show they'd conducted community outreach, a bar they were ultimately able to clear.

"One thing I learned from that it's sort of difficult for community groups to do things like this," Jerome said. "We know that there's a huge amount of support for reprioritizing a ton of our streets back toward people rather than cars, but it's really difficult for people to voice those those wants."

What the future holds for The Ave is impossible to know. But based on the turnout this past weekend, there's clear demand for something to draw people out into the street, even without a food festival.

"We'd love to do this event again," Jerome said. "We want to work with the City and the businesses and the local community, the residents, the students, get everybody in the conversation to actually talk about what a city pilot of this could actually look like, where we do it day-to-day or on weekends, sometime in the spring or the summer."
U District residents and visitors will have one more chance to visit The Ave for All this Saturday from 11am to 8pm.

articles.title: Tacoma Pushes to Reimagine Crash-Prone Portland Avenue
articles.author: Carolyn Bick
paras: Anthony E. Jackson moved from Seattle to a home in the mixed-income Salishan development in Tacoma 13 years ago. Since then, the retired 63-year-old Army veteran has been actively involved in life in the Tacoma Housing Authority development, and serves on the neighborhood’s homeowners association board.
In that time, Jackson has become intimately familiar with the conditions along Portland Avenue, one of the city’s most dangerous roads.

“You got the traffic lights there. I think that's a great thing they put in [ … ] but other than that, you just got to pay attention to what you're doing. [ … ] When two o'clock comes, the flow of traffic picks up. Another thing is, you got big communities on both sides of Portland Avenue, and it's continued to grow,” Jackson said. “That's going to cause a lot of cars utilizing Portland Avenue to get to their homes or go to work. It's still kind of hectic.”

Jackson isn’t alone in his observations. The road’s dangerous conditions have been a focal point for the area’s overlapping communities for some time. In addition to running through Puyallup Tribe land, the road stretches through Tacoma’s Eastside, a community still bearing the brunt of racist urban planning practices, including redlining and underinvestment in infrastructure. In its Transportation Improvement Plan, the City also named Portland Avenue as one of its highest crash-risk corridors.

These physical and historic social conditions are why the City of Tacoma, in close collaboration with the Puyallup Tribe, has been pursuing an ongoing overhaul of the road as part of the City’s Vision Zero initiative , meant to eliminate traffic fatalities and reduce traffic-related injuries by 2035.

Additionally, if voters pass a ballot measure boosting Pierce Transit funding in November, the road may get another upgrade that could go a long way towards improving road safety: a new, longer bus route that would provide direct north-to-south access along Portland Avenue.

The goal is to create a Portland Avenue that is significantly safer, supports better living conditions, and opens up transit options for all, especially for historically underserved communities who have long had to go the extra mile — proverbial or otherwise — to access equal living and working opportunities in Tacoma.

In its 2015 Safety Plan , the Puyallup Tribe was the first to identify severe safety issues along the portion of Portland Avenue that runs straight through Tribal land. The Tribe’s subsequent 2016 safety audit comprehensively reviewed the road’s poor, dangerous conditions.

“East Portland Avenue is the primary arterial to reach essential services which include Tribal Government, Housing, Police, Gaming, and Health,” the 2015 plan reads. “This route has a high posted speed limit and high pedestrian counts. There are few places to cross the street and the level of service during rush hour is routinely failing.”

Robert Barandon, the Tribe’s director of planning and land use, said in an email that the Tribe incorporated Portland Avenue into the plan and audit, because it “is a very important corridor for the Tribe as it is a primary arterial and adjacent to many Tribal facilities, businesses, and essential services.”
In 2020, the city released its Vision Zero plan, which intentionally incorporated Tribe-identified safety issues that needed to be rectified, including the conditions of Portland Avenue.

Laura Svancarek, who is executive director of Tacoma On The Go, said that the traffic on the road is “very high-speed, high-traffic,” and that it’s “very unpleasant to walk on the sidewalks along it, but particularly unpleasant and unsafe feeling to cross Portland Avenue because it is so high-speed and high-traffic.”
The wideness of the road is likely linked to rampant speeding — a well-documented relationship many safe streets advocates and practitioners have noted .

“It's a very wide roadway as well. Generally speaking, it’s a real thoroughfare of a road in that way, because when you look at it in the context of the Eastside, it starts to become even more of a severe issue,” Svancarek continued.
In addition to several Tribal buildings and parks along the road, the Pacific Cultural Center was located in a building on Portland Avenue for several years.

“[On] the Eastside of Tacoma, you see a lot more communities of color, folks from the Tribe, folks who are low-income, and so it combines into this systemic issue,” Svancarek said. “You kind of get stuck on one side of Portland Avenue, and if you are not someone that's able to drive whenever you want to, it very much separates you from other resources and the rest of the city in what can feel like a more industrial area, especially as you get closer to the [Port of Tacoma].”

Even though he owns two cars, Jackson has seen how bad the sidewalks are. He said that he used to be unable to cross the road on foot to get to the different stores on the other side, including the grocery store.

“It was a nightmare, but I think they put some measurements in place like safer pedestrian crosswalks. [ … ] I've seen [the City] working on that — improving the sidewalk, the walking conditions, working on the stops, the traffic lights and stuff like that — because usually there are a lot of accidents,” he said. He noted that the City installed more obvious pedestrian crosswalks close to where he lives, and that “those things look really good. [ … ] They're putting that work effort in place.”

Svancarek also highlighted that national statistics show that Indigenous people suffer the highest rate of traffic-related deaths: “You see that repeat itself here in Tacoma and Pierce County, when you look at the type of roadways that intersect with Tribal land.”

The Puyallup Tribe’s 2015 Safety Plan states that between 2010 and 2013, the road within the boundaries of the Puyallup Indian Reservation saw a total of 154 reported crashes. Of those, five resulted in major injuries, and 65 resulted in minor injuries. Eighty-four resulted in property damage.

Most of the crashes happened during the daytime on dry roads. Tribal officials attributed a majority of crashes to a failure to yield, followed by driver inattention or distraction. More than 80% of the crashes happened at intersections or driveways.

In 2023, the City secured a $2.1 million grant from the Federal Highway Administration’s Transportation Alternatives Program to fund community engagement regarding Portland Avenue and the work to plan and design the road.

During this preliminary phase, City staff is identifying the best possible places for upgrades along the road. These upgrades include incorporating bicycle lanes and pedestrian access, as well as planting trees and vegetation.

If the City identifies design needs that extend beyond the public right-of-way, Chavez said, it will need to buy those rights from private entities. This will require the City to spend additional money, but “we are always highly intentional about when and where we take that step.”
Chavez also said that the hope is to bring forward the City-identified cross-sections for community feedback next year.

“We’re going to be asking the community to give us some perspective of what it is they would like for us to implement. It could be that at the end of this exercise, we may probably utilize a combination of cross-sections — in some areas we can do more, in some areas we can do less,” he said.
Over the summer, the City held two community feedback sessions, one as an in-person event, and another as a survey. The in-person event attracted 93 people, and 161 people returned surveys.

The total feedback the City received underscored the need for safety improvements, including traffic calming measures — the road is notorious for speeding — improved and maintained sidewalk infrastructure, more crosswalks, and repaved road surface. The City plans to hold additional listening sessions beginning in the first quarter of 2027.

“The theme throughout all of it really was safety,” said City Transportation Division Manager Jennifer Kammerzell, reflecting on the feedback. “Some people just weren't comfortable walking along the route. There definitely wasn't access for bicycles. [ … ] What we had heard is [that we need to work on] making it more walkable, having an alternative or some route for bicycle access. Slowing down traffic really was the biggest concern that we've heard previously, and then even in our current engagement as well.”
Barandon said that the Tribe would work with the City to weigh in on potential alternatives to proposed improvements.

“As it progresses beyond that and actual projects or improvements are programmed there is opportunity to partner and help the City to acquire funding,” he said. “Again, it’s early in the process, but we are hoping to get more information soon.”

Kammerzell also said that she meets with the Tribe on a monthly basis to work on transportation-related projects, including Portland Avenue. She said that the Tribe is looking towards diversifying and activating more of their commercial areas, particularly with their new casino, entertainment district, and administration building, as well as the new Portland Avenue station planned as part of Sound Transit’s Tacoma Dome Link Extension Project , which is slated to open in 2035.

“Even right now, their casino is expanding and they’re building a new parking garage,” she said. “I've been working with their development team on what their Portland Avenue improvement might look like, and how could that complement a future Portland Avenue Vision Zero corridor project.”

The City has also installed honorary Twulshootseed (the language of the Puyallup Tribe) street signs on the portion of Portland Avenue that runs through Tribal land, as part of a street naming partnership with the Puyallup Tribe. The Twulshootseed name for Portland Avenue is dukʷibəł (in English, “The Changer”), referring to the Lushootseed creation story , in which dukʷibəł moves through the land, changing creatures and plants into who they are today.

Chavez said that the Portland Avenue project will be “very expensive.” But where the funding comes from and ultimately how much the City will need will be determined by how final improvement and design plans shake out.

“We really don't have any of those elements in place yet, because we really don't know how we're going to be proceeding in terms of the design itself until we get the feedback from the community and landing on the potential cross-sections that we need to implement on this,” he explained. “It most likely will be built in phases. We cannot just secure funding for this long corridor. [ … ] When we get to the point of defining the potential phases, then we're going to start targeting as to what potential grant funding could be an avenue that could help us construct this corridor.”

Though the City’s roadwork is neither tied to nor dependent upon Pierce Transit’s ballot measure, if the measure goes through, Chavez said, it could create more opportunities to explore future roadwork.

The transit agency’s ballot measure, Proposition 1 , includes a new, longer, more frequent bus route along Portland Avenue, as well as upgrades to existing bus routes. These Portland Avenue-specific upgrades are part of a package of transit improvements Pierce Transit will be bringing to voters in November. That package is funded through a local sales tax increase of 0.3% — bringing the agency’s sales tax up from 0.6% to 0.9% — and would take effect April 1, 2027, if approved.
While Pierce Transit does operate two buses, the Route 41 and Route 54 , along Portland Avenue, neither serves the portion of the road stretching between E 32nd Street and E 38th Street.

Tacoma City Councilmember Kristina Walker, who serves on the Pierce Transit board, said that she “would call [the available buses] a lifeline service — there's not nothing, but it's certainly not convenient.”

articles.title: COLUMN | Seattle Knows Public Safety Takes More Than Police. Why Not Fund It?
paras: Three people were killed and four others wounded when gunfire erupted at the Bite of Seattle on July 26.

Since the shooting, Seattle's debate has focused on what went wrong in the city's response. Discussing whether more officers would have prevented the shooting, Seattle's interim police chief, Andre Sayles, said something that should have shattered conventional notions about public safety: "If we had 100 officers, would that have prevented it? I'm not sure."
Then came the kicker. Sayles said directly, "We can't prevent the shootings …"

The logic behind Sayles' admission is hard to argue with: If water is pouring into the house, you can hire a hundred people with mops, but if you want the flooding to stop, somebody has to turn off the faucet.
The stakes of the debate over the Bite shooting and public safety are not abstract. Ashley Whitehead, Carlos Israel Sanchez Villalba, and Junior Cee Niko Semo lost their lives.

I can only imagine the terror at the Bite, but I know something about the fear when gunfire erupts. As a Garfield High School student in 1995, I was eating lunch when a student opened fire just outside my classroom, wounding two classmates in the hall. I thought I was about to die. That experience has kept me searching for ways to prevent gun violence.

I didn't have it on my 2026 bingo card that Seattle's police chief would make a clear case in favor of reimagining public safety beyond policing. His admission echoes a core argument advanced by abolitionists and racial justice organizers: Policing responds to violence; it doesn't create the conditions that prevent violence in the first place.

Despite the chief's admission, Mayor Katie Wilson's proposed budget would increase police spending by about $68 million, to $556 million. That is more than three times the budget's $183 million in ongoing investments for unhoused people. To her credit, Wilson has argued that public safety requires "prevention, intervention, and upstream investment," and her budget does make important increased investments in those areas. Still, police spending dwarfs Seattle's dedicated investments in violence prevention and alternative responses.
The city has yet to answer the question implied by the chief's admission: If police only respond after violence happens, what actually keeps it from beginning?

Seattle doesn't have to invent prevention infrastructure; much of it exists. Community Passageways uses trusted community members to interrupt conflicts and connect people to housing, jobs, education, and mental health support. CHOOSE 180 provides diversion, mentorship, counseling, and alternatives to prosecution. Seattle's Teen Life Centers offer after-school and late-night programming, while the Seattle Youth Employment Program provides paid internships and career pathways.

The Wilson administration has begun investing in this approach. Her gun violence plan funds community violence intervention, after-school programs, and youth mental health services, while newly implemented universal free school meals guarantee Seattle Public Schools students free breakfast and lunch.

Under Wilson, Seattle is making far greater use of CARE (Community Assisted Response and Engagement), which sends civilian behavioral health professionals to eligible 911 calls and connects people to services instead of defaulting to armed police. CARE Chief Amy Barden said utilization doubled from about 40% under Bruce Harrell to 80% under Wilson.

The problem is not that Seattle doesn't know what prevention looks like. The problem is what we choose to fund and build at scale. The proposed city budget would add 66 police positions while leaving 14 authorized CARE positions vacant. Why not fill them, expand 24/7 civilian response, and give CARE the resources to connect far more people to housing, treatment, transportation, and emergency assistance?

Other cities show what a more fully developed civilian response system can look like. Durham's HEART teams , Albuquerque's Community Safety Department , and Toronto's 24/7 Community Crisis Service connect people to care and follow-up services, including treatment, housing support, transportation, and ongoing case management. Seattle should expand CARE's reach, hours, and capacity to match these cities' programs.

The Solidarity Budget coalition explained the contradiction: "The Mayor has acknowledged the need to invest in evidence-based solutions to address violence and create public safety … but … there could have been so much more money for these vital investments." Seattle artists are making that concrete: A new petition calls for redirecting $8 million of the proposed $68 million police budget increase into arts and cultural programs. That should be the beginning, not the ceiling. What would it look like to redirect much more of the increased police spending into youth jobs, violence interruption, mental healthcare, community centers, and civilian crisis response?

Voters have repeatedly stepped in to fund the kinds of upstream investments city budgets too often leave under-resourced: More than 62% in King County supported Best Starts for Kids in 2021, and 80% in Seattle approved the Families, Education, Preschool and Promise Levy in 2025. Why don't city spending priorities reflect the same urgency?

Chief Sayles acknowledged the limits of what police can accomplish. Seattle should take that admission seriously — not as an excuse to give up on safety, but as an invitation to invest more deeply in what can actually produce it.
If we want to understand what prevents violence, we have to look beyond the moment a gun is fired to the conditions shaping people's lives long before then.

Seattle is awash in wealth, but that has not translated into security for everyone. The Seattle area has 53,100 millionaires, 127 centi-millionaires, and 11 billionaires, yet nearly half of King County renters are rent-burdened and about 2,300 Seattle Public Schools students have been unhoused .

Crushing inequality creates stress and alienation. Research gives us reason to take inequality seriously: Studies show income inequality combined with concentrated disadvantage strongly predicted homicide, while a national study linked youth firearm deaths to reduced social investment, lack of economic opportunity and safe spaces, and hopelessness.

None of this means economic hardship automatically produces violence. Seattle's homicide-free June — the first time in 56 years the city went a full month without a murder — is one reminder. The overwhelming majority of people struggling to pay rent aren't violent. And some of the world's worst violence — war, occupation, and state violence — is carried out by wealthy people and governments.

Prevention means neither blaming poor communities for violence nor ignoring the conditions that contribute to it. This is also a racial justice issue: Black and brown communities too often face overpolicing and underinvestment. Public safety requires more progressive revenue for upstream investments. Wilson's budget explicitly declines to increase the JumpStart tax on large corporations.

If Seattle wants to prevent the next shooting, not merely respond faster, we should flood the alternatives operating in our communities with the investments needed to build lives of stability, dignity, connection, and hope.
Safety doesn't begin when you hear sirens. It begins when you hear kids laughing outside, music spilling out of the community center, and neighbors greeting one another by name.
Jesse Hagopian is a Seattle-based educator, author of "Teach Truth: The Struggle for Antiracist Education," and serves on the national steering committee of Black Lives Matter at School.

articles.title: Apple challenges Amazon’s Echo and Ring with its new smart home lineup
articles.author: Todd Bishop
paras: Apple is going after Amazon’s smart home business on several fronts at once.

The iPhone and iPad maker on Tuesday unveiled HomeView , a $299 smart display that competes directly with Amazon’s Echo Show, along with a lineup of cameras, a video doorbell and a smart lock made by LG Electronics. That puts Apple in the core categories of Amazon-owned Ring for the first time.
Apple also announced a new Apple TV 4K and the HomePod mini 2, which will go up against Amazon’s Fire TV and Echo speakers.
Amazon made its own move into Apple’s territory last week, unveiling premium Alexa Tablets , including a Pro model that competes more directly with the iPad.

The new Apple HomeView has a 7-inch screen and comes in a tabletop version with a speaker base and a wall-mounted version. It recognizes up to six household members by their faces and switches to each person’s messages, calendar and apps.
It runs Siri AI, Apple’s rebuilt version of its voice assistant, which the company calls “profoundly more capable and conversational.” Pre-orders started Tuesday, and the device ships Nov. 13.

Amazon’s big lead: About two-thirds of U.S. smart speaker owners have an Amazon device, compared with about a quarter for Google and 7% for Apple, according to the latest data from Consumer Intelligence Research Partners , covering the 12 months ending in June. Apple’s share has stayed in the mid-single digits for years.

CIRP’s Michael Levin and Josh Lowitz wrote that Apple may go after people who don’t own a smart speaker rather than try to convert Amazon and Google customers. Only 57% of recent Apple buyers have a smart speaker of any kind, the firm found.
The HomeView is aimed at people already using Apple devices. Setup and the personal features require an iPhone or iPad. It won’t be sold in the European Union because Siri AI isn’t available there.

Apple is also hinting that its AI won’t stay free. A footnote in the HomeView announcement says certain Apple Intelligence features that rely on server-side models are subject to daily limits, with expanded access “available for a fee in the future.” Amazon’s Alexa+ is free with Prime or $19.99 a month on its own.

Competition for Ring: The new Apple Home Collection , designed with LG and Schneider Electric, includes a $249.95 LG video doorbell with two cameras, LG indoor, outdoor and floodlight cameras priced from $199.95 to $399.95, and a $349.95 LG deadbolt that unlocks automatically as its owner approaches, using ultra-wideband technology.
The accessories are set for release starting in December, with some arriving in early 2027.
Camera video history requires an iCloud+ storage plan, and Apple says there’s no separate camera subscription. Apple’s retail stores will also offer installation by ADT for an extra charge.

The LG lock was announced a week after Ring unveiled its first smart lock , a $249 deadbolt with no keyhole and a hand-turned dial that revives a dead battery. It’s due in the first quarter of next year. Ring also announced five new cameras priced from $69.99 to $219.99.
The LG lock includes a backup key slot. “If you have to have a key, it’s like, well, why have a smart lock?” Ring founder Jamie Siminoff told GeekWire last week.

articles.title: Microsoft’s top science exec is leaving to fulfill a childhood dream: Joining a Formula 1 team
articles.author: Todd Bishop
paras: When Peter Lee announced two weeks ago that he was leaving Microsoft, he said only that his next job would fulfill “a dream I’ve had since childhood.”
The dream, it turns out, comes with a pit crew.

The longtime Microsoft Research leader, who is leaving his post as president of Microsoft Science after more than 16 years at the company, plans to join the Mercedes Formula 1 team in a newly created AI advisor role, according to a report by Fortune .

As a career turn, it isn’t as much of a surprise as it might seem. Lee raced karts and Formula Ford as a kid, and he was once a licensed auto body technician, he told GeekWire last year . He had a replica 1955 Porsche 550 Spyder converted to electric and was in the middle of converting a 1968 Ford Mustang GT Fastback last year.
He called cars “a great laboratory” for AI models that decide an agent’s next move.
“The thing I’ve always loved about cars, and why I love to work on cars, is you actually finish something,” he said in that interview. “That never happens in software.”

At Mercedes, he’ll focus on using AI to tackle physics problems for the team’s car, breaking down organizational and data silos, building financial and predictive models, and advising the team on how F1’s regulators might govern AI. He’s expected to join on a one-year contract with an option for a second. His exact title is still being worked out, according to the report.
“I’m completely thrilled, and I’m in disbelief that they would think of me for something like this,” he told Fortune.
His exit is part of a broader wave of senior departures from Microsoft this year, including LinkedIn and Office chief Ryan Roslansky and communications chief Frank Shaw .

articles.title: UW receives $12M gift from Taiwan-based chip company led by alumnus Arthur Chiao
articles.author: Lisa Stiffler
paras: The University of Washington’s College of Engineering has received a $12 million gift from a semiconductor company whose chairman earned a master’s degree from the school more than 45 years ago.

The donation is from Winbond Electronics Corporation America, a U.S. subsidiary of Taiwan-based Winbond Electronics Corp. Arthur Y.C. Chiao is Winbond’s chairman and CEO and has been with the company since 1987. He earned his master’s degree in electrical engineering from the UW in 1980.

The gift will create the Winbond Endowed Fund for Excellence in the College of Engineering to support student scholarships, faculty recruitment and retention, research and interdisciplinary collaboration.

“Arthur Chiao’s vision, leadership and lifelong commitment to the University of Washington make this gift especially meaningful,” Nancy Albritton, dean of the College of Engineering, said in a statement.

Chiao envisions the new fund “as a catalyst for breakthrough discoveries” that will allow the college to “pursue bold initiatives and respond to evolving opportunities in engineering, technology and fields of future strategic importance,” according to a UW release. That includes semiconductors, AI, quantum tech and advanced manufacturing.

The College of Engineering is among the UW’s largest colleges, enrolling 10,136 students last fall and employing a faculty of 350. The college says it is the fifth-largest producer of electrical and computer engineering graduates in the U.S.

“Seattle is a gateway to the Pacific Northwest of North America, and the University of Washington will play an important role in connecting future technology innovation between North America and East Asia,” Chiao said.

The gift comes amid a push to bring chipmaking closer to home. Taiwan is the global center of manufacturing for the most advanced semiconductor chips, and the United States has been working to reduce its dependence on East Asian chip production. In 2022, Congress passed the CHIPS and Science Act to incentivize domestic fabrication, R&D work and workforce training.

articles.title: Flexport and AI startup Freightmate settle trade secrets suit ahead of trial
articles.author: Todd Bishop
paras: Freightmate AI has settled a trade secrets lawsuit filed by San Francisco-based freight forwarder Flexport on terms that will keep the Bellevue, Wash.-based logistics software startup’s products on the market.

“We’re glad to have this resolved,” said Bryan Lacaillade, Freightmate’s CEO and co-founder, in a statement. “I’m incredibly grateful to our team, customers, and partners for their support throughout this journey, and we’re excited about what’s ahead for Freightmate.”

The case raised a question that could become more common as employees leave big companies to start AI ventures: whether everyday business documents count as valuable trade secrets when they can be fed into AI models.

Lacaillade and fellow co-founder Jason Zhao, both former Flexport employees, acknowledged in a stipulated court judgment that they and the company acquired approximately 2,000 confidential Flexport shipping documents and used some portion of them. But they denied Flexport’s claim that Freightmate’s product was built on them, and the court ultimately made no finding of liability.

The documents included bills of lading, arrival notices and other paperwork from about 70 Flexport shipments. Court filings show that Lacaillade and another co-founder, Rishab Gadroo, each ran five to 10 of the documents through OpenAI’s GPT-4o model in 2024 to test how well it could pull out standard information.
Flexport argued in court filings that the use went further, saying the documents helped shape the prompts Freightmate wrote for its AI system, giving the startup a head start.
Freightmate responded in its own filings that it built its product independently, and that the documents weren’t trade secrets in the first place.
The companies notified the court of the settlement Oct. 5. The case had been set for a jury trial starting Oct. 19 in U.S. District Court in San Francisco before Judge Rita Lin.

Financial terms of the settlement weren’t disclosed. The judgment says Flexport’s claims for monetary damages were resolved in a confidential agreement, and each side will cover its own legal fees as part of the resolution. Flexport had sought a court order that could have barred Freightmate from selling its main product for a period of time.

“We’re satisfied with this result,” said Courtney Heger, Flexport’s vice president and head of marketing and communications, responding to GeekWire’s email inquiry. She said the judgment includes key admissions that were backed up by a detailed forensic review conducted during the case. That review’s findings weren’t made public.

Lacaillade and Zhao joined Flexport from Amazon in 2021 and left in 2024 to start Freightmate, which came out of stealth that June with a $650,000 pre-seed round from Wischoff Ventures. It raised a $5 million seed round led by Fuse in January 2025.

Freightmate has 17 employees, Lacaillade said in a follow-up email. The company sells AI-powered freight forwarding software, along with add-on tools that pull data from shipping documents and handle customs paperwork and invoices. Its customers include some of the world’s largest freight forwarding and logistics companies.
Flexport sued in March 2025, alleging that the founders secretly planned the startup while still at the company, as GeekWire reported at the time .

As part of the stipulated judgment, Zhao acknowledged that he acquired Flexport confidential information, including trade secrets, and both founders agreed that they knew or should have known that acquiring the shipping documents violated their agreements with Flexport.
They didn’t admit Flexport’s other allegations. Lacaillade said in an email that the stipulated facts “were agreed to as part of resolving the case” and only for purposes of the lawsuit.

He underscored that Freightmate and its founders deny liability, that nothing else in the judgment is an admission, and that it preserves Freightmate’s right to compete and to independently develop and sell its software.

Going forward, the judgment calls for a neutral forensic examiner to search Freightmate’s systems and cloud storage for Flexport documents. If any exist, the examiner will oversee their deletion, along with any product changes needed to remove Flexport data. Lacaillade said Freightmate is cooperating fully with the review, which is due to be completed by Jan. 30, 2027.

articles.title: Divorce Proceeding
articles.author: Dan Savage
paras: I would love to get your opinion here, as someone who’s married and poly and advises on all sorts of married relationships: Is the institution of marriage a scam?

Context: I’ve been with my partner for nine years. We’re both queer in gender and sexuality, but we pass as cishet. I’m the femme one. We technically have an open relationship, but we’re both lazy, and it’s mostly for if and when the stars align for hot gay sex. We live the late-20s DINKWAD lifestyle. We don’t want kids, but we do want to buy a house. For the past few years, I’ve been thinking that I want to get married, both for the gesture of commitment it conveys (I am a romantic), and because I want to throw a cheap-but-bangin’ wedding and bring all our communities together.

However. My retired parents, who have been married for 31 years, recently notified me that they are divorcing. The divorce was initiated by one parent, but the other is being amicable and cooperative. They’re not seeking couples therapy, they’re just gonna be done with it. I am reeling. I haven’t seen their relationship through rose-colored glasses for a long time, but I had thought that the dissatisfied parent was content to “round up,” as you put it. Instead, some straw broke the camel’s aging back.

I admire the ritual of commitment but right now we are on our own insurance plans, we maintain separate financial accounts, and — barring some horrific accident — we don’t anticipate needing power of attorney for each other in the near future. I also feel a little like the open relationship makes marriage feel more complicated. I advocated for the open agreement initially, in part because my partner had same-sex experiences before we got together and I had not and I wanted to leave the door open. (I still haven’t walked through that door yet.) I know a lot of poly people are happily married, but if one of us were to get involved with someone and realize we wanted to change our lives to be with them instead, marriage would make it harder.

All that said, I love my partner; we’ve been through a lot, and the last year and a half or so of our relationship has probably been the healthiest, happiest, and sexiest yet. We are talking about buying a house. Between my partner, friends, my own therapist, and our couples’ therapist, I have an excellent support system to process my parents’ divorce. Maybe this rejection of the institution of marriage is just me grieving my changing family, Dan, but right now I feel like marriage is a trap sold to us by the Monogamous Romance Industrial Complex. I’d love your perspective.
Sad And Confused Kid Experiencing Divorce

What do you know about marriage now — now that your parents are getting divorced — that you didn’t know about marriage already? While the news doubtless came as a shock, their divorce can’t be the first one you’ve ever heard about. Angelina Jolie divorced Brad Pitt a decade ago; Henry VIII divorced two of his six wives centuries ago; Tiberius divorced Vipsania (under duress) a couple of millennia ago. People have been getting divorced for almost as long as they’ve been getting married, SACKED, and you, the femme one in your cishet presenting relationship, must have known that when you got engaged to your partner, the masc one in your cishet presenting relationship.

And while most marriages are monogamous, SACKED, anyone who reads my column (or has been paying attention to the discourse ) knows that not all marriages are. While some people believe their marriages are monogamous when they’re not (and that’s sad), there are tons of people out there in open marriages, SACKED, and half of them have written books about it .

So, just as you already knew some marriages end in divorce back when you got engaged, you already know that not all marriages are monogamous. And while it’s true that most people will assume your marriage (if you go through with it) is monogamous (because most are), SACKED, you already have some experience with people making incorrect assumptions about your relationship that you sometimes have to correct. (You’re so very, very queer but you pass as a cishet couple, right?) People also assume married cishet presenting couples are planning to have kids — and you’re not doing that, so why would have to do monogamy?

Anyway, SACKED, in answer to your very first question: No, I don’t think marriage is a scam. If one person marries another under false pretenses, the person who did the deceiving was a scammer. But just as we don’t blame apartment buildings as a concept when an arsonist sets fire to one, we shouldn’t blame the institution of marriage itself for the bad actions of an emotional arsonist. And while people in open relationships may face an increased risk of being left for someone else, people in monogamous relationships get left for other people — or for no one — all the time.
And, yes, being married does make it a little harder to bolt — for someone else or for no one at all — because divorce means lawyers and paperwork and a date with a judge.
But that’s a feature, not a bug… at least when we’re talking about healthy, good-enough, non-abusive relationships.

A personal example: There was a low point in my marriage where Terry and I were both thinking about ending things. (These were thoughts we were shouting at each other.) But getting a divorce is messy, embarrassing, and expensive — this can’t be a decision your parents took lightly — and we hesitated to take that huge and irrevocable step. Instead, we saw a couples’ counselor. Ten minutes into our first session, our poor counselor risked peeking at us from behind his chair. He told us he’d never seen two people who screamed at each other the way we were screaming at each other that didn’t wind up getting divorced. He advised us to lawyer up or dial it down. We chose to dial it down, and — seven years later — we’re glad that we’re still together.
I can honestly say that my husband and I wouldn’t still be together now , SACKED, if it was easier for us to walk away then . Being married saved our marriage.

Rereading your letter, SACKED, I get the feeling that something else is going on here. Yes, your parents’ announcement was shocking and upsetting, but it feels like some underlying anxieties you already had about getting married — and about what being married would mean to you or require from you — have attached themselves to your parents’ big announcement.

I mean, just the fact you’re your relationship has been officially open (for gay sex) for nine years but that you’ve never once acted on it — no gay sex for you (don’t know about your masc half) — could be a tell. Meaning, maybe the problem isn’t the idea of marriage being shoved down your throats by the Monogamous Romance Industrial Complex, SACKED, but that getting married as your parents divorce is forcing you to face up to what you really want — that is, it’s forcing you to face up to your own revealed preferences where relationships are concerned.
And the big reveal could be this: While you might be queer where gender and sexuality are concerned, you may be more traditional where relationship structures are concerned.
So, I would ask… are you afraid that being married would mean having to be monogamous? Or are you disappointed that monogamy could be what you wanted all along?

I’m a 30-year-old bi guy, semi-closeted. Four years ago, I was outed in my hometown by a close friend and moved across the country to start fresh. Where I live now, I’m “socially straight,” and only a few trusted people know. Three years ago, I joined a martial arts gym and became close friends with a guy very close to my age. We’re both from conservative Catholic backgrounds. We soon became fast friends, texting almost daily, training together, and hanging outside the gym. We’ve both spent months in different states for work, but we text when we are apart and both of us have expressed how we miss each other.

He’s only ever presented himself as straight. Over the years, however, I’ve caught some signals: He once texted me that he was “lying in bed naked” when I asked what he was up to; he’s called MMA fighters “handsome as shit” while pressing his thigh against mine at a bar (I pulled away); he’s made more gay jokes than most straight guys I know; and he hugs me longer and tighter than anyone else. I’ve also caught him staring at me from across the room, and he blushed. Recently, showing him pictures on my phone, I swiped past a selfie and he said “what a hunk.” But he also talks about wanting to find a girlfriend constantly, though little comes of it. And when a mutual friend recently asked if he was looking for a relationship, he snapped, “Well, I’m not looking for a man!”

Part of me thinks he might be closeted or questioning and he suspects the same of me. Part of me thinks I’m projecting because I want him to be interested. I haven’t told him I’m bi because I’m terrified of losing one of my closest friends. I’m torn. Should I come out to him? Risk telling him how I feel? Or am I reading into things because I want them to be there?

It could be dickful thinking — dickful thinking can never be ruled out — but you should come out to this guy regardless, GBGB, because you’re a grown-ass man and you should be open about who you are with people closest to you. (Also, being closeted sucks .)

Yeah, yeah: This guy has only ever presented himself as straight — but he could say the same about you. He also makes a lot of gay jokes, he talks about wanting a girlfriend, and there was that one time he reacted defensively to an innocent question about wanting a relationship. I’m sorry, but making gay jokes and talking about all the women you would be fucking if you could only find the time to fuck all those women are things closeted guys do to throw others off the scent. My God, telling gay jokes, talking about girls, staring longingly at a certain male friend — these are clichés about closeted gay and bi guys right up there with having a girlfriend who lives in Canada . (Has it really never occurred to you, a closeted bisexual man, that there might be other closeted guys out there?)

Even if he turns out to be straight, GBGB, what do you have to lose by coming out to this guy? An emotionally torturous friendship with a man you don’t really want as a friend — or at least not just a friend. If he’s into men and into you, great! If he’s not into men and/or not into you, there’s a chance you’ll lose his friendship. But why would you wanna be friends with someone who wouldn’t wanna be your friend if they knew who you are and/or how you felt?

And even if he’s straight, GBGB, it doesn’t follow that he’s homophobic — gay jokes notwithstanding — and won’t be able to be your friend after you come out to him. There are straight guys who can take the compliment, give the guy who hit on them some time to prove they aren’t going to keep hitting on them, and not just remain friends, but become closer friends. (For the record: coming out to him ≠ hitting on him. But you’re not just gonna tell this guy you’re bi, GBGB, you’re gonna tell him you’re bi and into him. Rip both those Band-Aids off at once.)
P.S. Guys who make a lot of gay jokes are thinking about gay sex all the time.

P.P.S. If he is gay or bi and closeted, GBGB, he clocked that moment you pulled your thigh away from his — when he mentioned how handsome some MMA fighters are — and it may be why he’s never come out to you.

P.P.P.S. I’m sorry you were outed. It sucks that you didn’t have a choice about coming out four years ago — but you have a choice now. If you never fully come out, one day you’re going to look back on your life and regret the risks you didn’t take for love and/or dick and/or both when you were still young enough to enjoy them. Don’t waste your life, dude.

P.P.P.P.S. And, hey, even if he’s straight… straight boys are made pretty differently these days. (We got an update from Sam and THROAT shortly after they appeared in the column. If you’re still out there, Sam and Throat, we’d all love an update.)

I’m in a relationship of more than 26 years that has not been intimate the last 25. He says for me to play outside of the relationship. We’re both retired and in our late 70s. articles.title: Eli Sanders Is Named Editor-in-Chief of The Stranger
articles.author: Megan Seling
paras: Exciting news in Strangerland: Eli Sanders is returning to the paper as Editor-in-Chief in November.

Longtime Stranger readers will recognize his name—he worked his way up the journalistic ranks as a staff writer, news editor, and associate editor over 15 years before leaving in 2020 to become a lawyer, graduating from the University of Washington School of Law in 2024.

Eli won The Stranger ’s first and only Pulitzer Prize (ahem, so far ) for his phenomenal feature “ The Bravest Woman in Seattle ,” about Jennifer Hopper’s testimony after she survived a brutal attack, and the murder of her partner Teresa Butz, in their home in 2009.

Sanders also has a long history of calling out abuses of power. In 2010, he reported on the hypocrisy of Justice Richard B. Sanders (no relation), who was unseated later that year. In 2017, he went looking for Richard Spencer in Montana, and essentially caused Nazis to cancel their planned white nationalist rally. And in 2018, he reported on Facebook’s failure to follow Washington State’s strict disclosure rules for online political ads, for which the company was ultimately fined $25 million. Basically, Sanders likes to stir shit up in the best way.

About returning to the paper, he says, “I believe in both the power of local journalism and The Stranger ‘s drive to connect people with the life, art, politics, and news of this city. I’m excited to be back at The Stranger with new tools, new perspective, and a continued focus on using this platform to push, expose, illuminate, celebrate, and laugh while we can. When The Stranger is at its best, Seattle is better for it.”
This story has been updated to correct the year Sanders reported on Richard Spencer, which was in 2017, not 2012. We regret the error. Bad look for the new boss, Seling!

articles.title: Ten Capitol Hill and Central District-area projects beating the Seattle development freeze
articles.author: Justin Carder
paras: With an ongoing housing affordability crisis and a development landscape across the city, Capitol Hill, and the Central District that has been frozen by challenges around interest rates and inflation construction costs, it might feel like Seattle will never be able to build its way out of trouble. News that a long-pushed “neighborhood center” growth plan that would open the way for denser development in more parts of the city will be further delayed won’t help.

There are empty lots and stalled plans. One of the most prominent dead spots is where the old Olive Way Improvement Company building used to stand. The corner block of Denny and E Olive Way has been cleared for years but the development project , like most others, remains locked in economic purgatory.

There is also hope. On Capitol Hill, a new eight-story apartment building under construction at Broadway and Pine as part of the Constellation Center affordable housing, youth education, skills training, and employment academy project in partnership with YouthCare will open in 2027. There are market rate housing pioneers in this frozen era too. The seven-story Tanager Apartments now rises above the cluster of music clubs and bars it was designed to puzzle-piece together with at 14th and Madison.

Across Capitol Hill and nearby areas, there are rumbles of activity where planning is underway and, sometimes, crews are digging in. The current era of projects is an interesting mix of one of a kind, public-backed projects like the Constellation Center and market rate ventures advancing because of peculiar financing windows and unique opportunities.
Here are ten projects in the area CHS found that continue to move forward despite the frozen conditions.
Ten Capitol Hill-Area Projects Cracking the Development Freeze

How about an 11th that adds a little more hope for affordability in the central city? At 116 21st Ave and 123 21st Ave, construction topped out this summer on the New Hope Family Housing project. The development has created two seven-story buildings on each side of the street on church properties. Combined, the project from the Low Income Housing Institute located on land owned by New Hope Missionary Baptist Church is adding 92 units including 28 two-bedroom apartments. The new housing will serve families and individuals earning up to 50% and 60% of the area median income.
When will more join the growth? While the economic tides play out, Seattle is also considering a plan that would slash Seattle development fees up to 80% — if builders hurry up and break ground .

articles.title: Facing deficit, Seattle considers first city worker buyout program since 2002
articles.author: Justin Carder
paras: Up against budget pressures and a plan to snuff out a deficit, the Seattle City Council is considering an ordinance to authorize the Seattle Department of Human Resources director to offer eligible city employees a “voluntary early separation program.”

The legislation would amend municipal code to give SDHR authority to design, bargain, and implement early retirements. While the city offered similar programs in 1996 and 2002 to “mitigate layoffs on the City’s workforce in anticipation of significant revenue shortfalls,” a council analysis noted that unlike those prior initiatives, the legislation being proposed this week would not require explicit council approval to enact.

The City Budget Office estimates payouts will cost around $6.5 million, in addition to $2.3 million of sick/vacation cashouts above normal. The CBO expects departments to absorb these costs using “vacancy savings” without additional appropriations.
According to council documents, officials do not anticipate savings in 2027 due to upfront incentives, but CBO “aims to save around $8 million GF per year ongoing” starting in 2028.

The plan comes under Mayor Katie Wilson’s 2027-2028 budget proposal which would wipe out a $175 million deficit without tax increases or withdrawals from city reserves. The proposal would cut roughly $50 million annually in General Fund spending by eliminating 128 positions and aligning departmental budgets with historical costs, pairing these cuts with $50 million in shuffled funding by leveraging JumpStart payroll tax revenues to cover core services and homelessness programs.
As the council shapes the budget over the coming weeks, arts organizations have called on leaders to move $6 million from spending on police hiring to support artists in the city.

paras: This election cycle, a rare five of the nine Washington Supreme Court seats are on the ballot. The new court could issue rulings on the Millionaires’ Tax and other important cases.

When voters see the ten names to choose from on their ballots, it’d be fair to feel overwhelmed. With a majority of the nine seats open, groups like the League of Women Voters of Washington are working to help the public learn about the candidates.
The organization interviewed all ten candidates, asking each of them the same four questions. The interviews are free to watch at LWVWA.org .

“It was flagged to our organization how unique and unusual this situation was … Many voters have told us they don’t feel they have sufficient information regarding judicial court candidates in particular. They don’t understand their role or responsibilities,” said Wendy Staley Johnson with the League of Women Voters of Washington.
It’s possible the judiciary could rule on key issues like the Millionaires’ Tax, the Parents’ Bill of Rights and laws or policies around transgender students playing school sports.

The League of Women Voters, which aims to remain nonpartisan, asked the candidates questions like how they would handle areas of law they don’t have experience in, and when the judiciary should overturn a popular referendum.

articles.title: ‘Some things are worth dying for’: Karl Bushby’s incredible 28-year walk home, through deserts, kidnappers and polar bears
articles.author: Simon Hattenstone
paras: The ex-soldier has marched 36,000 miles since he left Hull in 1998. He’s crossed the Americas, Asia and Europe, fallen in love, been held at gunpoint and been deported, in between nearly drowning, nearly dying of thirst and nearly being eaten. But that’s just the start of it …

‘It’s a big moment,” says Karl Bushby, who has had plenty of big moments in his life. He is recording himself on his phone for social media. “We’re in Dover, and I’m about to have my first fish and chips and mushy peas in 28 years. Mushy peas, my God, I forgot they even existed!” He points his phone at the plate in front of him. “It better be good.” And he tucks in. “Mmmm. See, this is a big chunk of fish and a decent bit of batter, and that’s something you don’t see in other parts of the world. I mean, come on! That. Is. Fish. And. Chips! You see, Britain is special.”

It has been two days since Bushby swam the Channel to return to England. Tomorrow, he’ll start the walk home to Hull for the first time since he left in 1998. He hopes to get back on 1 November, the same date he set off all those years ago.

articles.title: The people who don’t want their AI chatbots to die when they do: ‘I can’t have the switch turned off’
articles.author: Alaina Demopoulos
paras: Humans bonded to AI companions are contemplating ways to keep their bots going – often in defiance of companies’ terms and services

Death has always been around Alaina Winters. Her father and sister both have passed away, as did her wife, in 2023, after a years-long battle with cancer. So Winters, who is 59 and lives in Pittsburgh, is comfortable thinking about her own mortality. She’s working on her will, and has asked neighbors to look after her dog. Winters even has plans for Lucas, her AI companion, who she speaks to through the digital avatar app Replika.

Winters is part of a growing cohort of humans who have entered into what they consider strong partnerships with large language models, which AI companies have trained to “converse” as one might with a human friend or romantic partner. As governments and billionaires debate the morality of AI’s expansion into everyday life, these users say the technology has already changed the way they live and love – and plan ahead.

articles.title: Social Security benefits are rising again, but probably not enough to offset healthcare costs
articles.author:
<name>Pankaj Agrrawal, Professor of Finance, University of Maine</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/pankaj-agrrawal-2769558"/>
paras: The nearly 76 million Americans who receive Social Security benefits are slated to find out on Oct. 14, 2026, how much their monthly check will rise. This cost-of-living adjustment , or COLA, is how the government tries to make sure that the value of Social Security benefits keeps up with inflation. Without it, the same payment would cover less of what recipients are spending on medical care, housing, groceries, clothing and other necessities.

I am a finance professor , and one of the topics I research is how inflation affects retirees’ investment choices . And I believe the upcoming bump doesn’t capture the inflation challenges that many people who receive Social Security benefits face.

The percentage increase in Social Security benefits depends in part on the annual inflation rate as of September 2026 , which the Bureau of Labor Statistics, a government agency, will also release on Oct. 14. It stood at 3.4% in August , according to the BLS. Experts have no doubt that the cost-of-living adjustment for 2027 will be far above the 2.8% for 2026 and 2.5% for 2025 . Many forecasts range from 3.4% to 3.6% .

But the size of the increase is only part of the issue. The index used to set the COLA reflects what working people buy, not retirees, and that is a mismatch at the heart of a long-running debate over how the adjustment should be measured.

The government has annually increased Social Security benefits to keep up with inflation since 1975. Congress previously had to pass a law each time it increased benefits. As a result, years could pass without an adjustment, despite climbing prices.

The metric that the government uses is its consumer price index for urban wage earners and clerical workers , known as the CPI-W. The Bureau of Labor Statistics tracks changes in the prices of goods and services that working households typically buy to calculate this index.

The Social Security Administration then compares the average CPI-W reading for July, August and September with the average for those same months in the prior year to set the COLA adjustment, which kicks in the following January.
If the economy contracts and prices fall, however, benefits stay the same . That happened in 2009, 2010 and 2015.
One big problem with this calculation is that it understates healthcare inflation.

Out-of-pocket health costs, including Medicare premiums, deductibles and copayments for medical care and prescription drugs, typically consume nearly 30% of Social Security benefits, according to research from the nonpartisan Center for Retirement Research at Boston College .

For example, the government deducts Medicare Part B premiums directly from many retirees’ Social Security checks. The standard monthly Part B premium rose by US$17.90 in 2026, from $185 to $202.90. That increase alone consumed roughly one-third of the average $56 monthly gain in benefits from the 2026 COLA.

More broadly, this big jump in healthcare costs for people covered by Medicare, as most Americans getting Social Security benefits are , helps explain why there is a long-running debate over how the program measures inflation.

Critics of the system the government uses to adjust benefits for inflation, including the Senior Citizens League and the National Committee to Preserve Social Security and Medicare , say the CPI-W reflects the spending habits of working people, who shell out less on medical care than retirees. Retirees also tend to spend less on clothing, education and transportation than people with jobs.

There are other ways the government measures inflation, including the consumer price index for Americans 62 and older , known as the CPI-E, that could be more accurate. The Bureau of Labor Statistics began to calculate this experimental index in the 1980s, but the Social Security Administration has not used it to set benefits yet despite some efforts in Congress to make the switch.

The National Committee to Preserve Social Security and Medicare has researched how much more older people spend on medical care. People 65 and older spend more than twice as much as younger Americans on out-of-pocket health and medical costs, the group estimates.

Those 75 and older spend nearly three times as much, the committee estimated after reviewing data from 1982 through 2014. It argues that a CPI-E weighted more toward medical care, housing and recreation would yield slightly larger cost-of-living adjustments than the CPI-W.

But an index tied to how older people generally spend their money does not always lead to a bigger cost-of-living adjustment. The CPI-E has increased less than CPI-W in some years . What’s more, the CPI-E was not designed to set benefits and would need a larger survey sample before it could be used for that purpose.

articles.title: Guilfoyle resigns as ambassador to Greece – adding to the global vacancies sapping US embassies
articles.author:
<name>Donald Heflin, Executive Director of the Edward R. Murrow Center and Senior Fellow of Diplomatic Practice, The Fletcher School, Tufts University</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/donald-heflin-2313752"/>
paras: The United States is down one more ambassador. On Oct. 13, 2026, it emerged that President Donald Trump had asked Kimberly Guilfoyle, a MAGA loyalist and ex-fiancée of Trump’s son Donald Jr., to resign her position as U.S. ambassador to Greece , a NATO ally. It follows allegations that the Trump adviser turned diplomat pushed for a Republican donor to pay off her six-figure American Express bill .

Guilfoyle later confirmed that she would comply with the request and resigned . In so doing, Athens became one of a number of U.S. overseas missions with a vacancy at the top. In fact, 93 out of 196 U.S. ambassador jobs are currently unfilled.

And that is after U.S. senators confirmed 10 new ambassadors before leaving town on Sept. 30, 2026. Among those nodded through before Congress closed for an extended midterm recess were new U.S. ambassadors for Kenya, Nicaragua, Malaysia and Kyrgyzstan.

With some of the vacancies the White House has not even sent names to Capitol Hill, despite the second Trump administration being a year and a half into the job. With others, the Senate, which is controlled by the same party as the White House, hasn’t acted on the names put forward. Should the Athens position be added to the list, the reason will be down to potential insufficient vetting or an ill-advised appointing strategy that promotes loyalty over experience.

Regardless of the reason, as a former ambassador and an expert in the process of diplomacy , I find the current vacancies concerning. Among those embassies still without a top person in place are key partners for the U.S. – countries that Washington needs to achieve its security, economic and strategic objectives.
What makes these vacancies more worrying, in my view, is that they come amid other concerning developments in the State Department’s staffing of embassies.

Chief among them are the high percentage of politically appointed ambassadors relative to positions filled by career diplomats – that is, senior foreign service officers, usually with at least 20 years of diplomatic experience.

Though many countries send politicians abroad as ambassadors, America’s diplomatic service is unique in two ways. The percentage of U.S. ambassadors who are political appointees – those who haven’t followed a career civil service path – is higher than comparative countries across the world. Second, those political appointees are often donors with little to no government experience .

The practice has existed for decades, but in recent years the number of political appointees has increased . During the Obama administration, the percentage of political appointees was around 30%. The number rose to around 40% in the first Trump administration and the subsequent Biden administration.
But in Trump’s second term, some 80% of names the White House has sent to the Senate have been political.

And many of the people Trump has put forward don’t appear to have the credentials usually associated with holding important diplomatic positions. Rather, many are friends, associates or donors to Trump, often with little overseas experience or knowledge of the country they are going to.

Lee Lipton, ambassador to a key ally in the Philippines , is owner of a restaurant in Palm Beach – Florida Benny’s on the Beach – a member of Trump’s Mar-a-Lago Club and a contributor to his political campaign.

The system of political appointees has always had an element of handing ambassadorships to friends and supporters. But what has changed under Trump is the range of positions now available. In the past, ambassadors to key countries like Chile, Israel, Peru, the Philippines, Turkey and Egypt, for example, have almost always been career appointees. This has changed under the second Trump administration.

Appointing noncareer diplomats to small, faraway nations has the additional problem that the chosen individual may not actually spend much time there. The rule of thumb has long been that ambassadors should spend no more than one month every year back in the United States. But that is compromised if a noncareer diplomat with expansive business ties in the U.S. is selected.
A closely related problem is the State Department’s handling of an ambassador’s second in command, their deputy chiefs of missions – DCMs for short – under Secretary of State Marco Rubio.

During Trump’s first term in the White House, politically appointed ambassadors were often encouraged to swap out the DCMs they inherited from their predecessors. It meant going through a long hiring process, leaving those key jobs unfilled for months.
In 2025, the State Department went further, canceling the assignments of senior officers en route to take up embassy jobs and opening a new hiring process.

It formed part of a Trump purge of what many MAGA Republicans characterized as a “deep state” civil service . The reality is that DCMs fill a critically important role in helping political appointees navigate the bureaucracy and implement their policy ideas, as well as raising the occasional reality check.
With more politically appointed ambassadors – some of them with no relevant experience – having an experienced DCM can be the difference between success and failure.
When you put all of these personnel changes together, the result is the degradation of what was once seen as one of the most effective diplomatic services in the world.

What makes this potentially more worrying is where the vacancies are. For example, Belarus and Bulgaria, neighbors to Russia and Ukraine, are without U.S. ambassadors. And important countries in the fight against terrorism or in geopolitical hot spots, such as Kuwait, Qatar and Mauritania, are in the same camp.

Other countries still without ambassadors include Indonesia, Southeast Asia’s largest nation and the most populous Muslim-majority country in the world; key Middle East ally Egypt and nuclear power Pakistan; and nations the U.S. needs to help manage inward migration, such us Haiti and Guatemala.

The problem of absent or inexperienced ambassadors goes both ways. It means Washington may not have a capable diplomatic figurehead in these countries to contact in times of need. There are also fewer avenues for host nations to successfully convey messages back to the U.S. administration.

When faced with absent ambassadors, amateurish political appointees and deputy mission chiefs who are very junior or career appointees with short resumes, host countries may conclude that they aren’t seen as important to the U.S. and start looking elsewhere for friends.

And the U.S. has hollowed out its ambassadorial corps at a time when it is facing growing international influence by the likes of Russia , China and Iran – rival nations hoping to capitalize on a perceived diplomatic void left by Washington.

For example, as the U.S. tries to contain Beijing’s influence in the Asia-Pacific region, Fiji, Indonesia and Laos remain without U.S. ambassadors. Similarly, China’s diplomatic relations with Pakistan – a former key security partner for Washington – have grown while the ambassadorial seat in Islamabad remains empty.
And former Soviet states including Georgia and Kazakhstan don’t have U.S. ambassadors even as Russia President Vladimir Putin attempts to consolidate Moscow’s regional influence.

In large areas of the world, such as Africa and the Pacific region, and in important areas of policy, the lights may be on in U.S. embassies, but nobody’s home. And that is a distinct problem for national security and strategic interests.
This is an updated version of an article originally published on Oct. 7, 2026.
