articles.title: I’ve been studying election integrity for 26 years, and here’s why I expect a normal election this November instead of chaos
articles.author:
<name>Justin Levitt, Professor of Law, Loyola Law School Los Angeles</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/justin-levitt-2236022"/>
paras: Fear of federal interference in the 2026 midterms , from intimidation stoked by armed officials at the polls to seizure of ballots, has been growing in the United States. That’s led state and local voting officials across the country to draw up plans for scenarios requiring them to summon law enforcement or prepare legal filings so they can keep the polls open .

In an interview with The Conversation’s politics and legal affairs editor Naomi Schalit, election law scholar Justin Levitt takes the temperature down a bit. Levitt says that while voting officials’ preparations mean they are doing their jobs, the anticipated election interference won’t happen – in part because of that preparation.
Schalit: Could we see widespread intimidation and challenging of voters at the polls?

Levitt: It’s extremely unlikely. I completely understand that Americans are freaked out . They are at an electric level of anxiety right now, not just about the world but about the coming elections. But I don’t think the intimidation and challenges they’re fearing or forecasting are going to manifest for a couple reasons.

I have run a nationwide election protection program . It’s real work to get people to dedicate a full day to helping others. It’s that much harder to recruit a group of people to show up and look for fraud, and fraud at scale doesn’t really happen . It’s even harder to recruit people to show up to actively intimidate voters.

Not that many people are in for it – there are keyboard warriors who love to act out online, but to actually show up is a totally different thing. And they’re really risking either getting thrown out of the polling place or going to jail, because intimidating voters is a crime .
What about intimidation and challenges by government officials?

On the government side, which is something people are also really freaked out about, we are a giant country and there are almost 100,000 polling places . The logistics of an intimidation operation don’t work countrywide.
To go from Step A, I’d like to intimidate people, to Step C, intimidate people everywhere? You’re missing a pretty giant Step B.

Here’s what I believe will happen: The federal government will send a group of a dozen goons to a suburban polling place somewhere, and they’ll have a camera crew with them. Bystanders will happily oblige them in filming. That clip will go viral and scare voters into not showing up at the polls because they think that there are individuals intimidating voters all over the place.
If people are worried about intimidation, go outside and see for yourself that in your neighborhood things are very normal. Even if social media depicts pure chaos.
Local and state election officials are preparing for mayhem or interference by the federal government . Are their efforts just based on overwrought imaginations?

No, they are being responsible. It’s their responsibility to prepare for everything so that the voters don’t have to worry about it. And they are as prepared as I have ever seen them. They’re preparing for a lot of truly outlandish scenarios , and some that are more realistic, so that they can be ready to make sure that the election is smooth and secure and feels very normal.
Could ballots be seized by state or federal officials?

Ballot seizure is also very much on people’s minds , and I think it’s particularly salient because the feds did it in Fulton County, Georgia , and because local sheriffs did it in Riverside, California. But there are two big reasons that’s not going to happen this fall.

First, the seizures in both Fulton County and Riverside were of old ballots. Fulton County’s ballots were 6 years old . California was more recent. It was a 2026 seizure for the 2025 elections , but those elections were still over and results had already been tallied.

That’s very different from an attempt to seize ballots while results are still pending , which is flatly unconstitutional . I just worked on an article with the former chief of the public integrity section at the U.S. Department of Justice. We did a lot of research and we think there’s never before been a federal warrant to seize ballot material when the results are pending. And that’s because judges don’t like to sign off on things that are illegal.

These seizures, in Fulton County and in Riverside, California, surely took the judges in those districts by surprise. Judges see applications for search warrants all the time, all day, every day. But warrants for election materials when the results are still pending are vanishingly rare. The warrants in Fulton and Riverside did us a favor because there are very few judges anywhere who are going to be surprised right now. Those seizures were big news .

In Fulton County, the judge allowed it , but he said very, very clearly this would be different if we were talking about a pending election where results weren’t still in the door. In California, the trial judge signed off on it . But the California Supreme Court came back just about a month ago, said this was absolutely, flatly illegal , there is absolutely no reason why a sheriff needs to seize these ballots. It is unlawful under California state law in a way that mimics other states’ laws too.

If somehow ballots get seized during the election process before they are counted and certified, that would mean that the chain of custody was broken and they would no longer be valid. Is that correct?

In the extraordinarily unlikely event that there’s actually a seizure, we’re in a little bit of terra incognita. It’s not entirely clear what happens. There will be immediate efforts legally to get the ballots back.

But the election system is built with belts and suspenders . If there’s a seizure of some materials, that doesn’t mean there’s a seizure of all materials or all materials relevant to a count. Sometimes there are paper ballots that are backed up by electronic copies , or vice versa. So what’s really important is that the election officials have a set of reliable records they can count.

The federal government may come in and say, “Give us the materials,” and the states are likely to say, “How about we make you copies?” And that’s fine. They can go off and have their copies and do whatever they want with them as long as the states are still able to count the records. It’s not really clear what would happen if there’s an extended lapse where the ballots are out of state custody. It’s not that those ballots are immediately invalid, but there’d be a fight about it.

I’ve been covering politics for a long time, and in the past 10 years the number of times we’ve gone into terra incognita was entirely unanticipated. Which is why I have to ask certain questions that seem completely implausible.

I’ve been working on elections for a couple decades now. My list of things to watch out for in 2000 was long. My list of things to watch out for in every subsequent election grew longer. The last couple of years, my list of things to watch out for has spilled off the page and onto the floor. For election officials, it’s a lot. They are stressed out, they’re underpaid, they’re overworked.
But all that said, they’ve got this. They’re actually as prepared as I have ever seen, including dealing with things that they haven’t ever seen before and should never have to be seeing.

I understand why people are afraid. I understand why people think there are risks. And that’s because it’s not normal to have the president fostering this much concern about the democratic process and who is this unattached to the democratic process.
But the good news is the process doesn’t depend on the president . It depends on us.

articles.title: More rehab centers should mean fewer overdoses. In one California region, we found the opposite
articles.author:
<name>Ilan Shrira, Associate Teaching Professor of Psychology, Penn State</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/ilan-shrira-2712178"/>
paras: At 24, Boyd was living in Chicago when he decided to get help. He had been drinking alcohol since a young age, but more recently he’d been drinking far more often – and dangerously.
He found a rehabilitation center online and reached out to the facility in Orange County, an affluent coastal area of Southern California, for treatment.

Boyd, a pseudonym used at his mother’s request, checked in at the facility, where he completed his initial detox and participated in therapy sessions. He was later readmitted to the same rehab program twice after his initial intake, his mother told the coroner’s office of the Orange County Sheriff’s Department.

Eventually he was moved to another nearby location operated by the same treatment program. However, despite the stated policy of sobriety on the treatment program’s website, Boyd began to use fentanyl.
In June 2024, two weeks after his final readmission, Boyd was found unresponsive in the bathroom at that facility, according to the coroner’s report.

He arrived at the emergency room in cardiac arrest; his heartbeat was restored, but he had minimal brain function, the coroner’s report later found. He remained on life support and died six days later.
The coroner’s office ruled his death an accidental fentanyl overdose.

Boyd’s story is not an isolated one. It points to a larger problem in the treatment industry. We are psychologists who research societal factors that contribute to overdoses. Our recent study found that out-of-state residents overdose in excessive numbers in Orange County, a hub for addiction treatment centers, compared with the rest of the state.
This finding runs counter to previous research that consistently shows that areas with more treatment facilities tend to have fewer overdoses .

In response to the opioid crisis in the United States, federal laws now require most private health insurance plans to cover addiction treatment. These laws have been mostly beneficial, providing millions of Americans access to treatment they otherwise could not afford.

However, the large amounts of insurance money flowing into the treatment industry have also attracted dishonest operators looking to score easy profits , especially in areas with weak regulatory oversight of treatment facilities.

A common scheme is to recruit patients with generous insurance plans to enroll at treatment centers , then bill their insurance companies for unnecessary or poor-quality services at inflated prices. These reimbursement payments can allow owners to pocket enormous sums of money , from a few hundred to US$3,000 per day for each patient.
These schemes are most profitable when patients have out-of-network private insurance, which tends to have higher spending limits.

Even the most generous insurance plans cover treatment for a limited time, perhaps a few weeks to a few months . Once that coverage runs out though, a patient who relapses can be readmitted to treatment, and the expensive insurance billing cycle can begin again.

This creates a perverse financial incentive for unethical operators to provide substandard care – or even interfere with recovery. Numerous investigations have documented how patients can become trapped in a revolving door of treatment, relapse and reenrollment, with each relapse putting them at risk of overdose and death.
Some patients travel outside their home state to receive treatment, and unscrupulous rehab operators often recruit such patients.

Their websites promise expert care and feature photos of luxurious accommodations. Prospective patients are sometimes given free one-way plane tickets, along with free housing and living expenses. There is even a market of third-party patient recruiters – or patient brokers – who get large kickbacks from treatment centers for each patient they bring to the facility.

Even when patients arriving from other states do not already have private insurance, they can purchase a California insurance policy as soon as they arrive. Patient brokers sometimes arrange this coverage and pay the insurance costs on the patient’s behalf.

People who travel long distances for treatment are particularly vulnerable to exploitation. Before arriving, they have little opportunity to see the actual conditions of the facility. Once they arrive, they are separated from their support network of family and friends back home, making them even more dependent on the facility.

When a patient’s insurance coverage comes to an end, they can be kicked out regardless of whether they’ve recovered . Patients who are far from home may not be able to afford the return trip. In some cases, they may face a difficult choice between homelessness or relapsing in order to stay in the treatment system that at least provides them with a place to live.
Orange County, California, has a large concentration of addiction treatment programs and has long been identified as a major center of treatment-related fraud.

California’s oversight of the addiction-treatment industry has been frequently criticized as inadequate , and the unusually large number of treatment facilities in Orange County makes misconduct even harder to detect.
According to 2019 federal data, there were 14 treatment centers per 100,000 residents in Orange County, compared with 5 per 100,000 residents nationwide .

One question we had was whether the large addiction treatment industry might contribute to more drug overdoses in the area. We reasoned that even if only a small fraction of treatment programs exploit patients, a larger industry would give rise to more of these programs – and potentially more overdoses.
We identified a 10-city region in Orange County with the highest number of rehab facilities, which had 35 treatment centers per 100,000 residents. We call this the study area.
We then compared overdose cases treated at the eight emergency departments in the study area with overdose cases treated at all of California’s other emergency departments.

Our analysis examined over 33 million visits to 323 hospitals throughout California from 2019 through 2021, the most recent data available when we began the study. To protect patient identities and comply with our data-sharing agreement, we can’t name the cities or hospitals in the study area.

To determine whether overdoses were unusually high or low, we compared them with bodily injuries, which is one of the most common reasons for treatment at an emergency department. In other words, bodily injuries served as a benchmark for the overall number of emergency department cases seen in the area. This approach can be useful when population sizes, such as the total population of visitors to the study area, are unknown.

Specifically, we compared the relative frequency of overdoses and injuries in the study area with the rest of California. A larger share of overdose cases in the study area would suggest overdoses were disproportionately high there.

We also identified how far people were from their homes when treated at the emergency department. We looked at three groups: Californians treated in their home counties, Californians who were outside their home counties, and out-of-state residents who were visiting California.

Emergency patients who lived in the study area were treated for 4,108 overdoses. Relative to injuries, overdoses were 10% higher than expected when compared with patients who lived in other parts of California. However, this effect was dwarfed by what we observed in the other two groups.

California residents who visited the study area were treated for 370 overdoses. Again, relative to injuries, overdoses were 68% higher than expected when compared to Californians who visited other parts of the state.

Finally, out-of-state visitors to the study area were treated for 316 overdoses. Here, overdoses were a staggering 159% higher than expected relative to out-of-state visitors to the rest of California.

One possible explanation is that the region’s many treatment centers simply attracted more visitors who are already struggling with addiction and thus more susceptible to overdose. We suspect there is some truth to this. However, we do not think it accounts for the more than twofold difference we observed between in-state and out-of-state visitors.
We believe this difference is at least partially the result of out-of-state visitors put at risk by predatory treatment schemes in Orange County, and especially in the study area.
Weak oversight has allowed these predatory schemes to persist in California.

The California Department of Health Care Services, the state agency that licenses and oversees addiction treatment centers, has been criticized as having lax regulations governing how most private-pay rehabs can operate.

The agency is also slow to investigate complaints, taking an average of nearly a year to complete most investigations and about three months to do so after a patient dies at a treatment center, according to an audit by the state.

In an email to The Conversation, a DHCS spokesperson said the audit covered fiscal years 2020-21 through 2022-23, “a period significantly affected by pandemic-related delays,” and that improvements to its investigation processes were already underway. The agency “proactively assigned staff to Orange County to address the region’s high volume of complaints and ensure timely investigations,” the spokesperson said.

A facility’s license can be revoked or suspended for extreme violations, but even in these cases its owner can continue to operate other rehab centers under a different company name and resume the same predatory practices there.

articles.title: Americans are stressed about grocery prices, so why do they toss or overlook so much ‘misfit’ food?
articles.author:
<name>Jintao Zhang, Assistant Professor of Marketing, Binghamton University, State University of New York</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/jintao-zhang-2769275"/>
paras: There’s a paradox that drives the shopping decisions of many Americans: Almost three-quarters say they’re feeling stressed out about skyrocketing grocery bills . But they keep discarding large quantities of food that’s safe to eat, from crooked carrots to surplus yogurt to “best before” items pulled from shelves early.

Overall, the U.S. government estimates that 30% to 40% of all food – from consumers, retailers and producers – is thrown out. That’s not just a massive missed opportunity for people experiencing food insecurity , but it’s also a significant contribution to global warming. According to the United Nations, 8%-10% of carbon emissions globally result from food waste.

In recent years, however, a market to rescue discarded groceries and repurpose food scraps and by-products has grown dramatically. This ranges from marketing “ugly” produce to appeal to more consumers to upcycling food by-products .

I study how consumers evaluate product value and quality, and my research suggests that American shoppers are much less fixated on prices or environmental impact. Instead, they care about quality. Even when perfectly good “misfit” produce is deeply discounted, for example, many shoppers assume that the low price reflects poor quality and either walk away or reach for a fruit or vegetable they think looks better.

What does this mean for reducing food waste and shedding these purchasing biases? My research has found that smarter and more effective labeling can make a big difference. A discount or promise of lower carbon emissions isn’t enough by itself – people have to believe the food is good first.

A whole retail sector is now dedicated to marketing misfit food. “Ugly produce” delivery companies like Hungry Harvest and Misfits Market are rescuing and reselling food to shoppers who want to save and reduce their carbon footprint. Misfits Market alone has rescued more than 265 million pounds (about 120 million kilos) of food since 2018 and sells it at an average discount of 35%.

Another example is Too Good To Go , an app that sells “surprise” bags of surplus food at about one-third of the retail price. It estimates that it has saved more than 26 million meals, including through partnerships with more than 530 Whole Foods stores . And the app Flashfood encourages grocers to list meat, dairy and produce nearing their best-before date at around half price and directs shoppers, including those on public food assistance, to those deals.

Consumers appear to be responding. Too Good To Go users in the U.S. saved 8.1 million meals in the first seven months of 2025, a 67% jump from the year before , while Misfits Market rescued 27 million pounds of food (about 12 million kilos) in 2025, up from 23 million (about 10 million kilos) in 2019, its first full year of operation.

This market is also using smarter labeling to grow its appeal. Shoppers who believe that food appearance is important tend to judge misshapen produce as lower quality. But labeling these offerings as “ugly” actually reduces that bias because it signals that the only flaw is cosmetic. Another study found that in-store messages that raise shoppers’ self-esteem can also make a different: In field tests, a “ Different Outside. Same Inside ” message successfully urged people to overlook external appearance when making judgments, whether on people or food.

This sustainability push is also playing out in the processed and semi-processed foods market, where would-be waste is converted into upcycled products. Examples include flour milled from soybean pulp, snacks that leave the fruit peel on, and “bites” made from rescued bananas .

Companies that want to market these goods can get third-party certification through Upcycled Certified if they pass an audit of their supply chain. More than 600 products from over 100 brands now carry it, and sales of certified products grew 17% from 2024 to 2025.

Here, too, perceptions of quality matter. In research on consumers’ acceptance of these foods, my co-authors and I found that they made their purchase decision based largely on whether they believed the product was as good as its conventional counterpart.

But in this case, in contrast to “ugly” produce, these products tend to be pricier, so they can’t compete through discounting. Rather, they usually sell at a premium – like this small bag of specialty flour going for $7. That means that it’s even more important they signal higher quality so they can appeal to less price-constrained shoppers.

Generational attitudes differ on this point, our research found . Gen Z, millennials and baby boomers are more willing to buy foods certified as upcycled if they agree that the quality and environmental appeal are worth it. But Gen Xers – those who were born between 1965 and 1979 – show less enthusiasm, citing a perception of lower quality.

That result fits what we generally know about Gen X shoppers. We discovered they are hard to persuade and cost-conscious, and they tend to rely much more on their own judgment. Gen Xers are also least likely to eat out or go shopping for groceries online, preferring instead to cook for themselves. That means they tend to scrutinize foods more closely in the store.
A “green” benefit won’t beat these skeptics. They need an assurance of quality from brick-and-mortar retailers they trust, rather than from online platforms.

The encouraging news from our research is that it sometimes doesn’t take much to change beliefs. In two experiments, my co-authors and I tested whether a simple logo could shift shoppers’ perceptions of foods made from rescued ingredients. We designed one version that was round, green and descriptive, following established design principles: Circular logos signal higher quality , while descriptive ones lift brand evaluations . The other was hexagonal, monochrome and bare.

We found that shoppers who saw products with the well-designed logo rated those foods higher in quality and were more willing to buy them than those who saw the same products with no logo. The poorly designed logo, meanwhile, made no difference.

It was the increase in perceived quality, in our view, that made people more willing to buy. A logo that looks credible, explains itself and signals care can change what shoppers believe. A forgettable one might as well not be there.

Closing this gap in perceptions, in short, doesn’t require shoppers to care more about the planet. It requires them to believe the food is good. The rescue economy can make that case, but it has to lead with quality and not only with conscience.

Jintao Zhang does not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organization that would benefit from this article, and has disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.

articles.title: Today’s irreverent politics ignore ancient wisdom: The need to know your limits
articles.author:
<name>Robert A. Ballingall, Associate Professor of Political Science, University of Maine</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/robert-a-ballingall-2696282"/>
paras: A common complaint today laments the “ shamelessness” of politicians . Until recently, the argument goes, more elected officials had a sense of shame to hold them back from ugly words and deeds, at least in public. Many in the current crop, however, seem to have no fear of disgrace ; they revel in contempt for the niceties of old – unwritten rules against cursing, slander or lying, but also written rules against abuse of power .
The problem isn’t so much a question of bad manners or even of corruption. It’s really about leadership.

I study the history of political thought and work on the psychology of lawfulness : the character traits citizens need for the rule of law to work. One such trait is each person’s ability to limit herself – to revere some larger principle that she would be ashamed to betray.

That’s all the more true for good leaders, even in a constitutional republic defined by checks and balances . Sometimes decisions need to be made over the objections of partisan opposition or of another branch of government. But the public can trust decision-makers only if those leaders check themselves.

Like many problems, political shamelessness may seem new, but thinkers stretching back to the ancient Greeks have warned of its perils, which they described as “irreverence” – the failure to respect something bigger than ourselves. If today’s politics seem threatened by some such menace, it may be because we are neglecting this ancient wisdom.
Perhaps the most searching account of this problem and what to do about it can be found in a work by the Greek philosopher Plato , who died in 347 B.C.E. The text is known simply as the “ Laws .”

Like his better-known “ Republic ,” the “Laws” envisions a “city in speech”: a utopia, a place that exists only in theory. But whereas the city of the “Republic” is ruled autocratically by “philosopher kings,” the “Laws” explores the possibilities and limitations of what is now called constitutional government.

All of Plato’s writings suggest that the most significant political fact is the scarcity of wisdom: the dearth of knowledge needed to live a flourishing human life. What’s more, he taught, most of us don’t recognize our own ignorance – indeed, we powerfully resist recognizing it.

Plato’s “Laws” examines the rule of law in light of this fact. It teaches that the function of law is to awaken citizens and politicians to their own ignorance and then to point them to a wise, ethical authority.
At its best, law wouldn’t just protect security or individual rights. It would provoke people to recognize their profound need of a standard of good and bad beyond their own judgment.

Otherwise, human nature being what it is, Plato saw that each person would corruptly “honor his own” – himself and everything connected to him – “ more than the truth .” He would rationalize his own prejudices and justify his own selfishness.

In the “Laws,” the antidote to this problem is what Plato calls “aidos ,” or reverence: the virtue governing shame, as well as awe. Taken by themselves, shame and awe are neither laudable nor blameworthy. But to have reverence, Plato suggests, is to feel these emotions for the right reasons.

Shame and awe go together for Plato because they both involve a feeling of diminishment: a sense of our own limits. With shame, this feeling is social, connected to the fear of someone else’s disapproving gaze. With awe, the feeling of smallness is inspired by something that makes our own concerns and capacities seem trivial – something like God or the divine.

It might seem as though a virtuous person would not feel shame; she would simply never do or say anything shameful. But in Plato’s eyes, precious few achieve so pure a virtue. For most, fear of shame is a necessary backstop to push people away from what wrongly tempts them. Likewise, awe prevents people from underestimating difficult tasks or from overestimating themselves.

According to the “Laws,” the proper object of reverence is wisdom, represented as God: “ the measure of all things .” The text stresses the awesome nature of the wisdom needed to judge things well – the need to look for truth outside ourselves. It teaches that we should be ashamed to “measure” things by reference only to our own fallible judgment.

Reverence might seem irrelevant to modern politics. In liberal democracies, public life is devoted to securing liberty, not to learning virtue. Shaming people for disregarding the awesome nature of wisdom might appear a gross violation of their freedom of conscience. Modern societies can scarcely agree on what is shameful to begin with.

Reverence might also seem to involve a piety that is out of place in a diverse democracy. Many people believe in God, but political decisions are judged by secular standards like their popularity, or by whether they benefit the public interest.

Nevertheless, I would argue that modern politics continue to depend on something akin to reverence. Liberal democracies might not use government to teach virtue directly, but they do need citizens and statesmen who appreciate the limits of their own judgment and their need of higher principles to guide their decisions.

It helps that awe need not be inspired by gods – or wisdom, which was what Plato truly revered. Citizens might feel awe, for example, at the enormous responsibility of self-government. As philosopher Jean-Jacques Rousseau wrote in the 18th century, democracy is more suited to gods than men : rightly understood, it is demanding in the highest degree.

Modern liberty is especially demanding; it isn’t only a matter of having a right to vote or speak our minds, as important as such rights may be. It is also a matter of having to choose between myriad ethical, religious and cultural traditions, or to choose none at all.
Such freedom is both a boon and a burden. In today’s democracies, citizens are responsible for their own ethical lives: for determining what should count as right and wrong, good and bad.

But it is precisely because we are free to waste our freedom, Plato might say, that we need reverence all the more: feeling awe for the responsibility of using that freedom well, and shame when we do not. As for political leaders, until they cease to find an approving audience for their contempt of principled behavior, the shamelessness that many observers find so disturbing will likely continue.

Robert A. Ballingall does not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organization that would benefit from this article, and has disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.

articles.title: Relaunched Community Court Gets Paired With Punitive Repeat Offender System
articles.author: Amy Sundberg
paras: The Seattle City Attorney’s Office (CAO) has announced two new programs affecting its handling of misdemeanor criminal cases in Seattle: a new community court called Connections Court and a new repeat offender system called the High-Priority Repeat Offenses (HiPRO) program. Both programs are being launched despite concerns expressed by the King County Department of Public Defense (DPD).

“Connection Court restores a key prosecution alternative with new accountability, and our HiPRO protocols seek firmer consequences for those who have taken advantage of Seattle's compassion,” Seattle City Attorney Erika Evans said in a press release.

Evans took office at the beginning of the year after delivering a rousing defeat to the former City Attorney, Republican Ann Davison. On the campaign trail, Evans promised to undo many of the harms of her predecessor, including beginning a new community court program to replace the one Davison had unilaterally shut down.
Less than ten months after taking office, Evans is delivering on that promise.

“Connection Court is a much-welcomed successor to its failed predecessors for importantly it centers on the participants and their needs but also accountability,” said Seattle Councilmember Bob Kettle, the chair of the public safety committee . “ I thank City Attorney Evans for furthering a more functional criminal justice system, which is crucial in creating a safer Seattle.”

Not everyone is as happy about Evans’ changes to this iteration of community court, the previous version of which was launched in 2020 by former City Attorney Pete Holmes. The biggest critic of the new programs is King County DPD.

Being the watchdog of CAO is nothing new for DPD, which spoke out against many of Davison’s policies. In addition to objecting to Davison’s ending of the former community court program, DPD opposed Davison’s High Utilizers Initiative and her Stay Out of Drug Area (SODA) and Stay Out of Areas of Prostitution (SOAP) exclusion orders . The department also drew attention to Davison’s enforcement of Seattle’s 2023 drug ordinance, which had a disproportionate impact on Black people based on City data and wasn’t resulting in the promised diversion.

Some hoped that with Evans in office, there would be a new ability of CAO and DPD to cooperate. But DPD told The Urbanist that Evans’ office didn’t inform them about the new HiPRO program until Monday, October 5, the day the new community court opened. As of Thursday afternoon, DPD hadn’t received any written protocols on the new system.

“I would say that we are disappointed by the HiPRO initiative and by the restrictions on who's eligible for Connection Court,” DPD’s Special Counsel for Criminal Policy and Practice Katie Hurley told The Urbanist .

On the criminal side, CAO only handles lower-level cases – misdemeanors and gross misdemeanors – while felonies are handled by the King County Prosecuting Attorney’s Office (KCPAO). In practice, this distinction means that many of the referrals CAO receives from the Seattle Police Department (SPD) involve crimes of poverty, oftentimes with a nexus of behavioral health conditions, although the office also handles some domestic violence and driving-under-the-influence cases.
Going forward, people who have been charged with a low-level, nonviolent offense without a pattern of repeated criminal misconduct may be sent through Evans’ new Connection Court.

“How I sum up Connection Court, it’s an opportunity to provide meaningful services to participants in the program so they get what they need to be okay, and then after 90 days, their case gets dismissed,” Evans told The Urbanist . “That is the summary of it, and I want it also really clear that we are still very robust in pre-file and post-file diversion, and this is just an additional layer.”

The new court program is being run at no additional cost to the City, providing an assessment with a court counselor to participants to determine which services would be the most appropriate for their individual needs. Evans talked about a menu of different services that includes medication-assisted substance use disorder treatment, help applying for health insurance, prescription delivery, mental health treatment, food, and ORCA cards. Participants will also have the opportunity to apply for jobs as downtown ambassadors with the Metropolitan Improvement District.

Evans is hoping to expand the program in the future, potentially hosting it at a local library and providing pet fostering for people who want to go into substance use treatment. And she has been in conversation with the Mayor’s Office about the possibility of setting aside a certain number of tiny homes or other shelter spots for participants in the program.

“I am very optimistic and hopeful that as we continue to grow and what we're able to provide for Connection Court, that the opportunity to have beds set aside for folks going through Connection Court is not only possible, but an absolute need for folks that are participating in the program,” Evans said.
Connection Court has a few key differences from its predecessor. These differences, which Kettle applauded, are points of contention between Evans’ office and DPD.

In the past, participants in community court would have their cases dismissed upon completion of the program, a policy supported by DPD. However, Evans has insisted on a 90-day jurisdiction period, regardless of how long the program engagements take, during which participants will need to avoid arrest in order to successfully complete the program. Participants also have to prove they’ve engaged with at least two different services.
Failure to meet either of these requirements and they could be sent back to mainstream court for criminal prosecution.

“We have to have a longer period to make sure we're actually engaging with participants,” Evans said. “I want to make sure that this is something that's going to be successful, and I know from us doing these cases, that's not in one day.”
DPD, on the other hand, believes cases should be dismissed when a participant successfully completes their engagement.

DPD also opposes stricter eligibility rules to the program. Evans has instituted eligibility restrictions for Connections Court based on prior criminal history, another change from the former community court. And Hurley said people will also be excluded if they are being held in custody for another offense, possibly because they are unable to afford their bail.

“We're really alarmed at that exclusion as well, as it denies the Connection Court pathway for people because they're not able to afford bail, and that's related to a case, a charge, where they're presumed innocent,” Hurley said.
Finally, people who are routed to the new HiPRO initiative won’t be eligible for Connection Court.

“These restrictions exclude the very people for whom a Connection Court is really most needed: those people struggling with homelessness, with behavioral health, who need support and help addressing underlying issues, rather than an aggravated jail sentence,” Hurley said.

The new HiPRO program will apply to cases where people who have been charged by the CAO either three times in three months or six times in six months. In addition, cases can be routed into the program immediately if a person has shoplifted in a store where they have previously been trespassed or if they’re being charged for a car prowl case (breaking into a vehicle) and have a conviction of felony theft, car theft, or robbery in the last year.
People with a case flagged for the HiPRO program will be ineligible for either diversion or Connection Court, and attorneys will ask for longer sentences for these cases.

“We're making sure we're giving folks opportunities for those services and treatment,” Evans said. “You know, one time, two times, and then I think it is important to have some accountability, you know, a third time. Otherwise, there is no incentive to [say], okay, maybe I should think about this and engage in some way.”
Hurley had a different view on the program, saying it will exacerbate current issues at the Seattle Municipal Court.

“They're going to be asking for aggravated jail sentences for low-level property offenses,” Hurley said. “Almost all of those folks are experiencing homelessness and/or behavioral health disorders, and it's going to be very expensive for the City. If judges were to impose these jail sentences, it's going to make it less likely that we'll be able to resolve cases and will likely result in more trials as we vindicate our clients' rights, and will make it so that we don't actually address the underlying needs people have. You're going to pay a lot of money for a system to try to punish folks whose basic needs aren't being met.”

According to the press release about the program, “this approach lets prosecutors dynamically target patterns of individual behavior, rather than relying on a static list of names.” The reference to a list is a clear recall to Davison’s High Utilizers Initiative , which was in fact a list of frequent offenders with more than 12 misdemeanor referrals in five years. An investigation by PubliCola in 2022 showed that most of the people on this list were unhoused and many were suffering from major behavioral conditions, with almost half ordered to undergo a competency evaluation.
Evans said anyone with a major behavioral condition should be going through the mental health court and doesn’t think her program will have the same issues as the High Utilizers Initiative.
Hurley said that in some ways, the new HiPRO program is more expansive than Davison’s High Utilizers program due to its inclusion of shoplifting and car prowling.

“I was exceedingly surprised to see a theft related to someone who previously received a trespass notice be considered a HiPRO individual,” Hurley said. “That is a low-level behavior involving a nonviolent property offense, which almost always has no actual loss to the store.”
The CAO will be adding the ability to track the HiPRO cases to its data management system , although it is not clear when this new capability will be operational.
Evans emphasized that CAO attorneys will have complete discretion around decisions about eligibility for Connection Court and which cases to include in the HiPRO program.
But Hurley said it’s important to design systems with policies that make sense for the majority of cases coming through that system.

“It's hard for me to imagine in my mind a case that would not be appropriate for Connection Court where a person is charged with a low-level shoplift involving a business, including a trespass,” Hurley said. “And if you're going to rely on individual prosecutors, line prosecutors, to make decisions, it's going to invite bias. It's going to invite unequal decision making, and it's going to result in far more people being excluded from these pathways than we saw under the previous iteration of Connection Court.”

articles.title: Seattle's 'Centers & Corridors' Zoning Update Delayed Another Year
articles.author: Ryan Packer
paras: The next phase of zoning changes planned to implement Seattle's twenty-year housing and job growth plan are on track to be delayed another year, according to a city briefing provided last week to the city's planning commission. A holdover from the Bruce Harrell administration, the " Centers & Corridors " zoning update had been set to rezone thirty new "neighborhood centers" for denser development and allow larger apartment buildings directly along transit corridors, but legal appeals have kept final approval at bay.
It doesn't look like that trend is set to change any time soon.

The appeals that have been assailing the environmental review underlying Harrell's One Seattle Comprehensive Plan since last February asserted flaws that have allegedly led to understated impacts from future growth on stormwater runoff, tree canopy, and other issues. But last month, a ruling from the state's Growth Management Hearings Board failed to find any evidence for those claims, upholding the way that the plan's final Environmental Impact Statement (EIS) was conducted.
But the board did throw the city officials a curveball that they're still grappling with.

Rather than studying "maximum likely development" under a future zoning scenario, the ruling stated, Seattle's Office of Planning and Community Development (OPCD) was required to analyze "maximum possible development", a fact that ropes in a significant number of housing units that are unlikely to be built in the plan's twenty-year horizon. Readjusting to study that maximum possible development expands the scope of the EIS considerably, even as the ruling itself acknowledges that Seattle is unlikely to see all parcels develop before updating its Comprehensive Plan again.

While the city was given a year to go back and fill in that additional analysis, any new zoning changes stemming from the EIS won't be able to be approved by the city council until the hearings board gives its stamp of approval. The deadline to get that analysis updated is September 9, 2027, with a compliance hearing scheduled for later that fall.

But despite the fact that OPCD is opening the EIS back up to do more analysis, there are no plans to adjust the city's preferred growth plan, despite what the aims of the appellants who had challenged it may be.

"The decision and order from the board is narrowly focused on the analysis in the EIS and what was, in their view, required to be in that analysis," Michael Hubner, OPCD's Long Range Planning Manager, told the planning commission last week. "We're certainly not bringing forward a new Comp Plan proposal, or any amendments to the plan based on this decision. And what's important is that the board did not order us to do so. The board did examine the Comprehensive Plan with respect to the issues raised in the appeal, and the city prevailed."

Hubner, who has been the planner sent to face community groups angry about seeing zoning changes brought to their neighborhoods, described the update that the city is required to make as a technical one.

"I think of it as really a technical add-in to our existing EIS, rather than changing anything fundamental about how we're planning for the next 20 years related to concurrent infrastructure investments, parks, all the things that the Comprehensive Plan addresses," Hubner said.

There are still a lot of outstanding questions that remain to be answered in the months ahead, including whether this additional required EIS work will impact Mayor Katie Wilson's attempt to go even further than the One Seattle plan when it comes to allowing additional density across Seattle's neighborhoods. Referred to as the "Taller, Denser, Faster" plan , Wilson's initial proposal has faced even more local opposition than Harrell's plan, but city planners had laid out a schedule that included potential adoption as soon as late 2027 – a schedule that now looks to be in doubt.
Could the city wrap up work on redoing the EIS well before the September deadline? Hubner described that as being unlikely.

"It's a pretty heavy lift to essentially add that information to the Comprehensive Plan EIS," Hubner said. "There's a lot of moving pieces there, so it's good we have a year, and we're starting to look at what it will take to update our analysis to meet the expectations of the board."

Updating the EIS to include these additional potential units would be a big enough lift for OPCD, but the hearings board appeal isn't the only challenge to the One Seattle Plan still alive. The same day that Hubner provided his update to the planning commission, Seattle's hearing examiner held a conference to discuss a set of city-level appeals that continue to advance on a parallel track.

Filed by Seattle symphony performer Jennifer Godfrey (who also filed the growth hearings board appeal) and Mount Baker lawyer John M. Cary, those two appeals have been trying to stop the One Seattle Plan in its tracks since last February. But changes in state law relating to exemptions under the State Environmental Policy Act (SEPA) caused the hearing examiner to dismiss both challenges, a dismissal that was ultimately reversed after further appeal to the state's Court of Appeals. That ruling seemed to affirm a major loophole in SEPA exemptions that applies to environmental review that hasn't yet been acted upon by a legislative body.

But there's another twist. Though the hearing examiner's office now has the appeal back in front of them, they may be forced to dismiss it again, following the approval of a bill approved this summer by the Seattle City Council that removed the path of city-level SEPA appeals for area-wide rezones and Comprehensive Plan amendments. Proposed by land use committee chair Eddie Lin, the bill proved very divisive and passed on a 5-4 vote , despite the fact that other jurisdictions including Bellevue, Tacoma and King County do not allow this path of city-level appeal.

Though it was initially unclear if that new law would apply retroactively to appeals that were already active, the hearing examiner has already dismissed another appeal on the grounds that the office now lacks jurisdiction, a challenge to the city's plans to keep housing prohibited in the Stadium District . While that suggests dismissal could occur here as well, the examiner hasn't yet ruled on that question.

"One of two potential things could happen: the hearing examiner will grant that motion and dismiss, and be appealed, or the hearing examiner will hear the appeal on its merits again over the next number of months," Hubner said. "We're looking at a calendar for the case that stretches into early next year potentially."

The exact schedule for those two appeals would likely be a bigger deal if OPCD wasn't already scrambling to address the Growth Management Hearings Board ruling. But a hearing on the merits, should they reach that stage, could potentially force additional changes to the EIS on top of those, extending the process even further.

While all of those legal issues continue to play out, Seattle's zoning framework – where midrise affordable housing projects are only legal to build on 3% of the city's land – will stay in place indefinitely.

articles.title: Robot on aisle 7: Customers react to autonomous inventory machine roaming a Seattle grocery store
articles.author: Kurt Schlosser
paras: Shoppers navigating aisles of chips and cookies at a Fred Meyer store in Seattle’s Greenwood neighborhood are dodging more than carts — they’re also sharing space with a smooth-gliding, autonomous robot named Tally.

Equipped with an array of cameras, computer vision and AI, the slender machine pauses briefly near display shelves before beeping like a grocery-focused R2-D2 and zooming down the line to scan digital shelf tags.
During a GeekWire visit one morning last week, Tally sparked a mix of curiosity and pointed questions about the impact of retail automation from shoppers and workers alike.

“It’s kind of wild,” said a shopper named Mark, who, like others we encountered, preferred to give just his first name. “It’s the Jetsons happening right here, right now. If this is what the future is then I guess that’s what it is.”

The future apparently arrived a couple years ago, at least as far as Fred Meyer parent Kroger is concerned. The retail giant began piloting robotic technology in 2024 to “gain real-time insights on product inventory.”

According to a thread on Reddit , Tally robots have been spotted in Fred Meyer stores in Seattle as well as around Washington state, including in Lynnwood, Puyallup, Port Orchard and University Place. Kroger operates more than 50 multi-department grocery and retail stores across the state.

“At Fred Meyer and QFC, we are always exploring new and innovative ways to create a more convenient and friendly customer experience,” Tiffany Sanders, head of public affairs for QFC & Fred Meyer Divisions of Kroger, said in an emailed statement to GeekWire.

Sanders said the technology means “associates can more easily and quickly identify and address shelves where products are low or out of stock” and that teams gain more time “to do what they do best,” which is serve customers.

Sanders did not provide any details about how many stores in the region are using the robots, how many hours per day they roam the aisles, whether any human workers have been displaced, or what Kroger does to ensure customer privacy.

Cincinnati-based Kroger’s automation push does come amid plans announced Monday to slash roughly a third of its corporate workforce over the next three years under a sweeping restructuring led by CEO Greg Foran to lean heavily into technology and streamline operations.

Developed by San Francisco-based Simbe Robotics , Tally is an autonomous mobile robot engineered to help retailers track inventory, check pricing accuracy, and monitor product placement using computer vision and AI. Standing more than 6 feet tall with a slender frame atop a rounded Roomba-like base, the robot navigates store aisles at slow speeds using dozens of onboard sensors designed to safely weave around shoppers and displays.
Rather than sounding alarms or pinging workers in real-time, the robot feeds data into Simbe’s software platform, generating prioritized task lists for store employees to handle out-of-stock items.

Introduced to the market in 2015, Tally is part of a growing wave of automated inventory technology competing for space in grocery store aisles nationwide. Rival systems include autonomous machines from competitors such as Badger Technologies—whose googly-eyed robots are deployed in chains like Stop & Shop—as well as software platforms from companies like Brain Corp.

Simbe has scaled rapidly alongside competitors, recently surpassing a milestone of 3,000 autonomous units under contract globally, anchored by a 500-robot footprint within Kroger’s nationwide ecosystem.

Autonomous robots like Tally may patrol grocery aisles on their own, but some tech companies argue that the best way to track inventory isn’t by adding another machine to the floor, but by empowering the humans already there.
One Seattle startup taking that approach is Augmodo , which develops spatial AI technology designed to capture shelf data through human movement rather than roaming robots.

“Augmodo started by knowing what is actually on the shelf, just like robots, but our vision is to augment the physical workforce,” said Augmodo founder and CEO Ross Finman . “People already go up and down the aisles hundreds of times a day, so enabling the existing workforce with simple, inexpensive smartbadges can provide more frequent, cheaper data while also building an AI assistant to add two years of experience to every associate across back of store, delivery, facility maintenance, and more.”
Unlike autonomous floor bots that have drawn privacy scrutiny from shoppers, Finman emphasized that Augmodo’s hardware focuses strictly on products rather than people.

“Regarding privacy, we focus on products, not people — we actively filter out any people before anything leaves the store,” Finman said. “We do not just filter out anything that could be a person, we filter out anything that is irrelevant.”
Ranked No. 122 on the GeekWire 200 list of top Pacific Northwest startups, Augmodo raised $21 million in a funding round this summer, a year after raising $37.5 million .
For all the futuristic promises of automated inventory , the machines still invite a mix of skepticism from those who share the floor with them.

During GeekWire’s Fred Meyer visit, a number of shoppers gave the robot a bit of side eye or muttered at it for being in the way while they shopped. At one point, Tally paused for several minutes in front of an aisle end cap stocked with Doritos. In other aisles it easily maneuvered around floor displays or paused for customers.

“Right now, it’s a curiosity,” said a Hershey sales rep named Mike who frequently stocks candy in grocery aisles and has watched Tally navigate the store. While he noted that the robot doesn’t personally bother him, he echoed rumors heard among workers about potential labor impacts.

Other shoppers looked past the novelty and expressed concern about broader privacy implications. Patrick, a Seattle resident who works in cybersecurity, said he usually tries to avoid the aisle when he spots Tally rolling past.

“First off, it’s taking jobs, but also it’s just more mass surveillance,” Patrick said . “Every time I pass it, I wonder: Is it collecting Bluetooth pings off your smart devices? … I’d be very surprised if it really was just doing cameras on the shelves versus trying to collect data on actual customers as well.”

The anxiety over data collection comes at a sensitive time for major grocers in the region. The Seattle City Council recently passed a groundbreaking ban on algorithm-based “surveillance pricing,” prohibiting retailers from using personal data and AI tracking to set individual, dynamic prices for shoppers.
Simbe’s Tally website features images of shoppers posing for selfies with the robots, under a headline that reads, “People are more likely to shop at retailers with in-store robots.”

While Tally is officially engineered for inventory management, shoppers like Patrick say roving robots only deepen distrust over how much corporate data is being gathered inside the aisles. Pointing to the cameras mounted on the robots and pairing them with modern AI tracking software, Patrick argued that it feels reminiscent the pushback against Flock automated traffic enforcement cameras.
“I think it’s just another way for them to cut the humans out of the labor force and steal more data from customers,” he said.

articles.title: Why Amazon might pay billions for Decart, a 3-year-old AI startup that hasn’t disclosed its revenue
articles.author: Todd Bishop
paras: A deal for Decart , a startup that makes software to help AI models run faster on different kinds of chips, would give Amazon new ways of getting more AI developers to use its custom chips instead of Nvidia hardware.

The Wall Street Journal reported Sunday that the companies are in talks for an acquisition that could value Decart around $7 billion, citing people familiar with the matter. Amazon and Decart haven’t confirmed the talks. Amazon hasn’t responded to GeekWire’s request for comment.

A deal of that size would rank among Amazon’s largest. The company paid $13.7 billion for Whole Foods in 2017 and $8.45 billion for MGM in 2022, and in April it agreed to buy Globalstar , a satellite company, for $11.57 billion.

It would also be far larger than the deal that started Amazon’s chip business. Amazon bought Israeli chipmaker Annapurna Labs in 2015 for a reported $350 million. That team went on to design Trainium and Amazon’s other custom chips, now linchpins of its cloud business.

Decart hasn’t disclosed its revenue but has been profitable almost from the start, according to the business publication Globes . Its customers include eBay, which is also an investor, according to Bloomberg . CTech reported that Decart’s business remains far smaller than the valuation being discussed.

Nvidia dominates the AI chip market in large part because of CUDA, the software that developers have used for years to build and run AI models. Moving that work to other chips, including Amazon’s Trainium , normally takes extra engineering work.

What Decart does: Decart sells software that makes AI models run faster on chips from Nvidia, Google and Amazon, and makes it easier for developers to switch between them, according to the Journal. It licenses that technology to cloud providers and AI labs.

The company also builds its own AI models, including Lucy, which edits live video in real time, and Oasis, which generates interactive virtual worlds. Brothers Dean and Orian Leitersdorf founded Decart in 2023 with Moshe Shalev. The company is based in San Francisco, with a development center in Tel Aviv.

For Amazon, owning Decart could make Trainium an easier sell. Customers with AI models built for Nvidia chips could run them on Trainium with fewer changes, and Amazon would get the engineers behind the technology.
Decart’s software could also help Amazon get more out of the chips it already has. That was Anthropic’s goal in pursuing the startup, according to Bloomberg .
The company’s video models could fit other Amazon businesses, too. Streamers use its technology on Twitch, which Amazon owns. Its Lucy model can show online shoppers how clothes look on them.
Existing ties to AWS: Decart has already moved its own models to Trainium.

At AWS re:Invent in Las Vegas last December, Decart’s real-time video model turned AWS Senior Vice President Peter DeSantis into a live cartoon of Amazon CTO Werner Vogels on the side screens as he opened his keynote. It was a joke about taking over a morning slot that attendees expected Vogels to fill.
When Decart CEO Dean Leitersdorf took the stage later, the model animated him, too, mimicking his movements. The animations were generated live on Trainium3, Amazon’s newest AI chip .

Leitersdorf said the startup worked with AWS to move its models and infrastructure to Trainium. Amazon said that week that Decart was running real-time video four times faster on Trainium at half the cost of GPUs.

Earlier suitors: Amazon isn’t the first company to pursue Decart. Anthropic was in talks to buy the startup for about $6 billion, Bloomberg reported in August , and Nvidia held acquisition talks before that, according to the tech publication CTech .
Nvidia also invested in Decart’s $300 million funding round in May, which valued the startup at about $4 billion.

Anthropic walked away in September after due diligence, Bloomberg reported, adding that the companies may still work together in other ways. Globes, citing sources close to Decart, reported that the founders had refused Anthropic’s push to move much of the company’s team from Tel Aviv to San Francisco.

Anthropic is one of Amazon’s closest AI partners. Amazon has invested about $18 billion in Anthropic and could invest up to $15 billion more as certain milestones are met. Anthropic uses Amazon’s Trainium chips to train and run its Claude models.

Larger industry moves: Amazon isn’t alone in trying to reduce its reliance on Nvidia. Microsoft on Monday unveiled Maia 300 , the third generation of its custom AI chip, and said it plans to make Maia the main hardware for running AI in its own products starting in 2027.
Google has its TPU chips, and OpenAI has developed a chip with Broadcom.

A deal for Decart could come together soon, according to the Journal , unless talks fall apart or another suitor emerges. One open question is whether Decart’s software would keep supporting Nvidia and Google chips under Amazon ownership.

articles.title: Stranger Suggests: Your Agenda This Week, October 12–18
articles.author: By Julianne Bell, Amanda Manitach, Charles Mudede, Emily Nokes, Audrey Vann, Shannon Lubetich, and Surprise Paradiso
paras: (MUSIC) Synthy darkwave duo Boy Harsher returns to Seattle for a two-night stand after last performing here in 2022. In the four years since, the band’s members ended their romantic relationship and released their fifth full-length record, Get Mean . The album explores the moody turmoil that follows a breakup while the two find ways to bring out the creative best in each other, with vocalist Jae Matthews describing it as a “complex emo time” in her “wild hallowed life.” Considering everything, I find it particularly fascinating that the album artwork is a photo of themselves from 2021 where their faces and lips are touching intimately. Underground pop princess True Blue and experimental industrial band Kassie Krut round out the lineup of artists whose music encourages dancing through the darkness. Time to break out your faux leather jacket and thick black eyeliner! ( The Showbox, 8 pm, all ages ) SHANNON LUBETICH
Neal Stephenson Presents ‘D: Heavy Water’

(LITERATURE) No one does a sprawling narrative universe like Neal Stephenson. His novels usually contain enough information to make you briefly believe that you, too, could understand orbital mechanics, cryptography, nuclear physics, or whatever special interest he’s bringing to the adventure this time. I’m a huge fan: Seveneves and Fall; or, Dodge in Hell are two of my favorite science fiction works by a contemporary author. When I saw his 2024 book, Polostan , was a historical-fiction spy novel, I was skeptical (for selfish reasons—I was hoping for another 900-page sci-fi epic to transport me out of our current tech nightmare and into a much more interesting one). But, as Baroque Cycle readers already know, Stephenson’s an entertaining historian—I flew through the story, which follows a young spy-in-the-making and moves between the Soviet Union and America in the interwar years. (There’s a stop at the 1933 Chicago World’s Fair that’s particularly fascinating.) Polotsan is the first in his Bomb Light series; its sequel, D: Heavy Water , picks back up in 1930s Europe where journalists, spies, scientists, and government officials scramble to control a substance crucial to the coming atomic age. Stephenson’s superpower is making enormous concepts and systems feel thrilling, and I, for one, am ready to go on this ride. ( Third Place Books, 7 pm ) EMILY NOKES

(LITERATURE) Wake up babe, David Byrne’s new book about his creative process, Sleeping Beauties , just dropped. The Talking Heads frontman’s latest endeavor explores his concept of “sleeping beauties,” which refers to slept-on ideas that don’t gain traction until long after the creator is gone—the most obvious example of this is Vincent van Gogh, who famously sold just one painting in his lifetime. In his new book, Byrne digs into how these ideas “fell asleep,” how they can “wake up,” and the importance of not overlooking the next great idea. ( Meany Center for the Performing Arts, 7:30 pm, all ages ) AUDREY VANN

(FILM) Exactly a year ago, I was in Eastsound for what I consider to be the best film festival in the Pacific Northwest, the Orcas Island Film Festival. The day was cool with brief blasts of rain. I met people leaving a No Kings protest at Green Park. I watched a number of top-tier films. And one night, after drinking at the Barnacle, I experienced the kind of rain and wind that can only be described as numinously autumn. This year, the festival again has top-tier films, thanks to OIFF’s on-it team, which includes SIFF’s former chief curator and director Carl Spencer. To name a few: There’s Clarissa , a modern-day adaptation of Virginia Woolf’s Mrs. Dalloway (it’s set in Lagos, Nigeria, and stars David Oyelowo). And there’s Paweł Pawlikowski’s gorgeous Fatherland , which stars Sandra Hüller and concerns one of the giants of modernist literature, Thomas Mann. And there’s Andrey Zvyagintsev’s Minotaur , which exposes the moral rot of neoliberal Russia by examining the marriage of a wealthy but unhappy couple. If you need a quick but wholly satisfying break from Seattle, this festival will not do you dirty. ( Orcas Island, 11 am ) CHARLES MUDEDE
Rocky Horror Picture Spooktacular Tour with Patricia Quinn

(FILM) I will never forget the first time I saw Tim Curry as Dr. Frank N. Furter step out of the elevator singing “Sweet Transvestite” in fishnets and a sequin corset. I was 13, at the Admiral Theater’s monthly midnight screening of The Rocky Horror Picture Show , and I felt deeply confused and excited by my first crush that existed beyond gender. This, my friends, is the bi experience. As the years have passed and monthly screenings diminish, I fear that teenagers are not being exposed to the magic of Rocky Horror . Take this opportunity to introduce the virgins in your life (in RHPS speak, that’s someone who’s never seen the film) to absolute pleasure with a special appearance from Magenta herself, Patricia Quinn. ( 5th Avenue Theatre, 7:30 pm, all ages ) AUDREY VANN
somesurprises & Ilyas Ahmed w/ Morgan Henderson

(MUSIC) Formerly the bedroom project of singer-songwriter Natasha El-Sergany, somesurprises has evolved through the years into a dynamic duo with synthesist and guitarist Josh Medina, blending soothing folk with electronic elements and shoegaze-inspired fuzz. Their latest EP, Year Without Spring, is appropriately reverbed (which, in my opinion, is a lot of reverb) and will most definitely sound amazing in the Good Shepherd Center’s spacious Chapel Performance Space. They will be joined by Portland-based experimental artist Ilyas Ahmed and multi-instrumentalist and Stranger Genius Award short-lister Morgan Henderson (Blood Brothers, Fleet Foxes). For fans of: Broadcast, La Luz, Mazzy Star, Phoebe Bridgers, and Slowdive. ( Chapel Performance Space, 7:30 pm, all ages ) AUDREY VANN
Refract 2026: Through the Looking Glass Tour

(VISUAL ART) If you’ve ever yearned to deepen your knowledge of the region’s glass scene, gather with glassholes, or dabble in the hot shop yourself, let Refract be your guide. The annual festival takes place at galleries, museums, and studios across the greater Seattle area. Sample the hottest young glass artists in town (like Yale Wolf, Megan Stelljes, and Henry Jackson-Spieker) in Refract: Local Frequencies at The Space Columbia City, get hands-on making your own decorative autumnal squash at SLU’s Seattle Glassblowing Studio, or get downward-dog amid Chihuly’s many-tentacled splendors during a yoga class at the Chihuly Garden and Glass Museum. My top picks, however, are the intimate artist open studio sessions with masters of the craft like Carol Milne, Morgan Madison, and Weston Lambert. ( Various locations ) AMANDA MANITACH

(FOOD & DRINK) My fellow Fall Bitches, I have found the best PSL in the city, and it’s at Tailwind Cafe in Capitol Hill’s Chophouse Row. Tailwind lovingly crafts their (vegan!) pumpkin spice syrup in-house, blending quality ingredients one might expect (actual pumpkin puree) with some that might surprise you (pancake syrup). The result is both familiar and divine. Spiced velvety foam gives way to a smooth, hearty body. The finish is mildly sweet but never cloying, and ground clove and cinnamon linger on the tongue even after the last sip. If last season is anything to go by, PSL season ends at Tailwind when they run out of syrup, so get yours soon! ( Tailwind Cafe, 9 am–7 pm ) SURPRISE PARADISO

ENTER NOW! Contest ends October 13 at 10 am
Baba Obscura Pioneer Square, November 5–8, 21+

articles.title: Is Mayor Katie Wilson Still a Socialist?
articles.author: Charles Mudede
paras: This story begins with Mayor Katie Wilson’s proposed $9.1 billion 2027-2028 budget . It matches estimated revenue with estimated expenditures. It is, in other words, a balanced budget. And the way she accomplished this feat has attracted attention from all quarters. Unlike Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s balanced budget , Wilson’s has no new taxes or tax increases. The rates for the JumpStart Payroll Expense tax, a progressive tax she helped design and went into effect on January 1, 2021, have been frozen .

In a KUOW interview with Wilson on Tuesday, reporters questioned why Wilson didn’t raise JumpStart to fill Seattle’s $175 million budget deficit but instead relied on cuts “somewhere in the range of one to 8% to a lot of departments, including the Department of Transportation, Office of Housing, Seattle Public Utilities.” Wilson’s answer? “We really believe in the power of government to make lives better, to make people’s lives better,” she said. “And I believe that the real foundation for that is trust in government, and also really responsible budgeting.”

By all appearances, this balancing act cannot be described as progressive. Indeed, it’s receiving high marks from Seattle’s business community , who see it as a sensible budget for a city that, according to mainstream media, does all that it can to ruin the business climate. Furthermore, evidence of leftist anti-realism is revealed by Seattle’s job market, which has contracted significantly while Bellevue’s and Tacoma’s have expanded (the former by a lot; the latter, a little ). The scales have finally fallen from Katie Wilson progressive eyes (or her idealism).

Now, let’s put aside the fact that the tech sector as a whole is presently bleeding jobs (and so Seattle’s contraction has little to do with taxes). Let’s also put aside the fact that in our society, whether a balanced budget is mandatory or not, it’s frequently the left that worries about balancing budgets (in this regard, Katie Wilson is like the former mayor Mike McGinn , another progressive who was a budget hawk). The right, as is made evident by Republican presidents, and particularly the present one , don’t care about deficits if they result from tax cuts for the rich or accelerated military spending . Balancing the budget only matters when it concerns social spending.

Let’s also, and finally, put aside another fact: Deficits from social spending actually benefit the economy because members of the working class do not save or hoard or remove money from circulation by purchasing paper on capital markets, but, as all Keynesian economists well know , instead send what they earn or receive from the government right back into the economy. In the words of a great but underappreciated economic thinker, Billy Paul , workers and the poor “let the dollar circulate.”

What I want to focus on instead is something expressed in the headline for Wall Street Journal ’s article on Wilson’s budget: “Seattle’s Mayor Ran as a Socialist. Then She Ran Into Reality.” This matter about her breaking with her socialist principles was brought up repeatedly by David Kroman in a recent KUOW interview with Wilson. Considering her budget, and its across-the-board cuts, and its increase in police spending, could she still consider herself a socialist? In the words of Kroman: “You have famously called yourself a socialist, but… frankly, this does not read as a socialist’s budget. So, are we witnessing a political evolution of Katie Wilson here?”

To be honest, the mayor’s response to this question was, at the end of the day, vague, though she did assert that she had “[a]bsolutely not” changed, that she was still a socialist. Nevertheless Wilson and her team prioritized “getting out of this cycle of annual budget shortfalls.” Kroman was not the only one to question her commitment to socialism. The WSJ reported that centrist Seattle City Council member Bob Kettle, a former cop and the current public safety committee chair said that Wilson “isn’t governing like a Democratic socialist” because she can’t. “The realities of sitting in the seat and doing the job, you have to deal with those realities, Kettle said.” (The late cultural theorist Mark Fisher called this kind of thinking “ capitalist realism .”) Former socialist council member Kawant Sawant, appeared at a public hearing for the budget this week and excoriated Wilson, calling her a “self-described socialist” because “she delivered a budget that cuts public sector jobs and essential services and gives a shocking $68 million to the Seattle police.”

Sawant considers herself a “revolutionary socialist.” What does this mean? How is it different from being just a regular socialist? Though Sawant is famous for leading the way to higher local, regional, national wages, and relentlessly pushing for higher taxes on the incomes of billionaires and millionaires, goals of this nature are not actually revolutionary (which, in Sawant’s context, entails the complete transformation of society into something radically new—a society without capitalism). But high wages and progressive taxes are connected, ultimately, with what is called Ricardian Socialism .

And what’s the essence of this economic philosophy? It stems, weirdly enough, from the thought of an early 19th-century millionaire (today he would be a billionaire) and conservative David Ricardo, who insisted in his 1817 book On the Principles of Political Economy and Taxation that labor is the source of value, not capital. Now, if you put one and one together, you realize that if labor creates value then labor, under capitalism, is being robbed of its wealth by the rich. What Ricardian Socialists want is not a revolution but a fair share of the capitalist pie. This is Mayor Zohran Mamdani, Sen. Bernie Sanders, and even Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed, who is not anti-capitalist but anti-poverty, anti-low wages, and pro-affordability and the universalization of healthcare. If labor is the source of wealth, then it deserves more social benefits.

This is where things get interesting. Though Marx admired Ricardo and expanded this labor theory of value considerably, he made it clear in his later works that labor was not the historical subject of capitalism or value. Capital was all about capital. And so his books were mostly an analysis of this economic system: how it works, how it goes from booms to busts, how it transformed value, a social substance, into profits. Though there is not much in his books about socialism, he does, in his notes, collected as Grundrisse , see the future society that follows capitalism as one that takes advantage of capitalist technological innovation to increase, for workers, “disposable time.” Yes, Marx is all about that time, free time, time to develop your mind or your mastery of a guitar or turntables or knitting. This is not a joke. Marxist futurology privileges disposable time, time away from work.

Marx’s own words : “What capital adds is that it increases the surplus labour time of the mass by all the means of art and science, because its wealth consists directly in the appropriation of surplus labour time; since value directly its purpose, not use value. It is thus, despite itself, instrumental in creating the means of social disposable time, in order to reduce labour time for the whole society to a diminishing minimum, and thus to free everyone’s time for their own development.”

To be honest, I rarely hear socialists in positions of power or influence (revolutionary or not) mention disposable time, time that’s paid for in the basic income sense, time for an individual’s self-improvement or intellectual/artistic/creative growth. Indeed, the only person to bring it up recently is none other than the billionaire Jeff Bezos. A few days ago, he went on Fox News and, according to Forbes , “said he believes artificial intelligence could generate enough productivity gains to allow Americans to have a three-day workweek or rely on a single-income for the whole household—pushing back against fears that the technology could lead to large-scale job losses for American workers.” This is as pure as Marxist futurology gets.

Now, as to whether Bezos is serious about this or not, I will play it safe and go for the latter. As to whether Katie Wilson is a socialist or not, I can say for certain she is not a revolutionary socialist like Sawant. As for her being “a self-described socialist,” well this is the case with all socialists because there are no rituals or formal ceremonies that confirm or consecrate your allegiance to this political program. As for her proposed budget, no matter how you cut it, it’s a bit of a bummer.
