articles.title: Slog AM: MOHAI Workers Unionize, Trump the Environmentalist, and the Nobel Peace Prize Nods to Gaza
articles.author: Cedar Attanasio
paras: Good morning ya frigid bastards. It is 40 degrees Fahrenheit (4 degrees Normal) this morning, and I am so excited for the cold (read to the end to see why).
The news is also full of silver linings and upside-down logic.

Take it from an Italian: It may be “Columbus Day” in much of the US, but you wouldn’t know it in Seattle, where it is strictly Indigenous Peoples’ Day. Check out Daybreak Star today starting at 4 p.m . if you want to celebrate anything.

Seattle’s time capsule of oppressive labor practices is getting a union! Visit the Museum of History & Industry—MOHAI—and you can learn about the Capitol’s oppression of labor in the logging, longshoreman, and scuba diving industries, all sponsored by techno whip-wielding Florida man Jeff Bezos. Perhaps that history inspired the museum’s workers toward a labor win? They announced recognition of their union last week, charting a worker-friendly course for the future.

Less grocery means more grocery. Amazon Go, Bezos’s failed cashierless convenience stores, are going away. Yay! Plenty of pixels have been spilled over grocery store closures in the Seattle area. But one Amazon Go closure, in Ballard, won’t leave a food desert. It is opening up a culinary oasis in the form of Seattle’s first Hashi Market, MyBallard.com reports . I haven’t been to Hashi Market, but reviews suggest it’s like a cross between a Japanese H-Mart and a Muji.

Agents with ICE raided a Democrat’s home in Minnesota: Rep. Ilhan Omar’s house was raided by Homeland Security Investigations agents, ICE’s detectives, according to NewsNation via The Hill and others . This is not normal. This is not right. So close to the election, this is election interference.

What other ICE shenanigans can we expect ahead of the election? Anecdotally, credible reports of Immigration and Customs Enforcement arrests in Seattle were up this week, according to ICEOUT.org and some of the more reliable Facebook groups. I’m keeping an eye on immigration enforcement for The Stranger these days, so if you are a trained ICEwatch rapid responder, or really know your shit for some other reason, reach out on Signal: “StrangerICE.206”

Meanwhile, the Washington Sun reports that DHS is mulling no-bid combat training for ICE from UFC . The motherfucking Ultimate Fighting Championship, operated by TKO Group Holdings, is unlikely to provide guidance in de-escalation tactics.

Pollution into the Sound from the Port Townsend Paper Co. wasn’t investigated by the Washington Department of Ecology. If you missed the news about this massive pollution spill into the Puget Sound, it could be due to a cover-up, according to detailed reporting from the Seattle Times . A worker who took videos and photos of the spill says the pollution was underreported, reminding us that no news is not always good news. The whole incident reveals how much the state relies on companies to police and regulate themselves.

America’s warmonger president spent the weekend complaining he wasn’t getting the Nobel Peace Prize. Writer/sugar baby Colin Jost captured the president’s vacuous naivete on SNL: “He did so much war that we’re running out of missiles, and he still thought ‘this is my year.'”

The Nobel Peace Prize went to Navi Pillay , a champion of international norms and human rights. Pillay grew up under apartheid in South Africa and lawyered for activists like Nelson Mandela, says the New York Times . Last year, she chaired the UN commission that concluded Israel had committed genocide in Gaza. Her next project focuses on genocide in Myanmar. Is she coming for Zuck ?

Washington is pedestrian-friendly, according to Camilo Ruiz, a guy who walked from Orlando to Seattle. The Florida Man, who lugged a cart for 213 days, strolled into Issaquah this week, and made it to the Space Needle over the weekend. Walking from the burbs into Seattle, he said, “One thing I love about Washington is how pedestrian-friendly it is.” Congratulations to us.
A security guard was killed outside a Seattle strip club, and a young woman was shot in the leg. KING5 reported the drive-by shooting happened around 1 a.m. Sunday.

Despite decades of buying weapons from the US, Saudi Arabia is not able to protect itself from the poorest country in the world. Houthis have been lobbing missiles from 500 miles away in Yemen with brutal, lethal results. Over a dozen people were killed and hundreds more injured in a series of attacks on the Riyadh airport on Saturday and Sunday, Reuters reports . Video from the airport shows many of the victims were religious pilgrims headed to or from Saudi Arabia’s holy sites like Mecca and Medina.

The fatal attacks on Saudi Arabia out of Yemen are ultimately Trump’s fault , and a foreseeable consequence of the war in Iran. So despite his poor marks in peace class this year, Trump will ultimately join this additional front in the war, The Guardian thinks. Can’t put Jared’s investments at risk!

But here I am, consoling Trump. Don’t worry, buddy, Nobel Peace Prize winners have also been pretty murdery. Barack Obama won the award and went on to bomb a fellow peace prize winner, Doctors Without Borders . Henry Kissinger got it after bombing everybody .
Back to consoling myself, about the cold. Here are the shiver linings:
1) Our hiker/climber/etc. friends are BACK and joining us for indoor fun. (Twenty people showed up to the juggling night at the Ballard Community Center on Wednesday.)
2) It’s scuba diving season. That’s right! We dive more in the winter because reduced algal blooms and less glacial runoff make for better underwater visibility.
Here’s some Canadians explaining why “cold as balls” is something we look forward to.

articles.title: Indian-style Pizza Rasoi lands inside Capitol Hill’s Outer Planet Brewing
articles.author: Justin Carder
paras: Capitol Hill’s only nano-brewery now has a pizza counter with global flavors. Pizza Rasoi is serving inside 12th Ave’s Outer Planet Brewing .

Founded by Maahir Kasliwal , Pizza Rasoi is kind of like if you beamed up a slice and a curry at the same time, mixing the energy fields of an Indian kitchen into pizza. Chef Kasliwal’s creations center on hand-crafted dough topped with aromatic curries and marinades, pitching each pie as “a bold Desi twist on your favorite comfort slice.”
Pizza Rasoi directly translates to “Pizza Kitchen.”
Kasliwal’s venture has grown as a pop-up and with its first spot located inside South Lake Union self-serve bar Tapster .
The Capitol Hill menu now being served at Outer Planet features $20 medium pies anchored by chicken and housemade paneer options across regional profiles.

The lineup includes classic Tikka atop a “rich and creamy tomato tikka sauce,” Achari dusted in a “Mustard and fennel forward pickling spice blend,” Hariyali finished with sliced jalapeños and julienne ginger on a “rich and herby spinach and cilantro puree,” and a cardamom-tinged Malai sauce, alongside a Lasooni chicken tikka featuring a “bright yogurt herb base” topped with “confit garlic” and garlic oil.

The arrival of Pizza Rasoi on 12th Ave adds to the street’s slice selection. The Brunton brothers opened Roma Roma in February with Roman-style pizza sold by the pound in the space formerly home to the Capitol Hill Racher’s Ginger Beer .
The new addition is part of new growth at tiny Outer Planet w hich celebrated new ownership last fall as beer maker Amory Carhart took over the 2015-born microbrewery wedged in beneath microhousing.
Pizza Rasoi is now open inside Outer Planet Brewing at 1812 12th Ave. Learn more at pizzarasoi.com .

articles.title: ICE on Capitol Hill again? Video appears to show federal stop outside Capitol Hill’s City Market
articles.author: Justin Carder
paras: Video appears to show ICE agents taking a person into custody outside City Market as word spread of federal immigration activities on Capitol Hill Monday morning.

The video posted around 9 AM shows tactical law enforcement personnel gathered around the open driver’s door of a sedan parked in the market lot along Bellevue Ave with an unmarked dark patrol vehicle stationed directly behind it. The vehicle is pinned by the unmarked enforcement cruiser directly behind it in an operation that unfolds in broad daylight alongside passing morning neighborhood activity, including a stopped yellow school bus and nearby pedestrians.
The officers are clustered inside the open driver’s side doorframe of the car, either restraining or handcuffing an occupant or taking someone into custody near the vehicle.

While the clip is labeled as an “I.C.E.” operation, the tactical gear and unmarked vehicle could also be federal task force or regional units, making the exact agency unconfirmed from the visual evidence alone.
CHS is checking with officials to learn more.

In August, CHS reported on a video showing an operation on 10th Ave E involving similar agents. In that video, one officer dismisses questions, stating, “I’m not getting into this with you guys” before remarking, “Biden hired me. I don’t know what to tell you.”
Regional spokesperson for ICE Alethea Smock did not respond to our previous inquiries about operations in the neighborhood.

Reports from efforts like the Washington Immigrant Solidarity Network show that U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement field operations have continued across Seattle and the broader Pacific Northwest.

articles.title: New Flyover Video Shows Latest West Seattle Link Design
articles.author: Ryan Packer
paras: Sound Transit has officially reached the 30% design milestone on the West Seattle Link project, celebrating the occasion by releasing a new flyover video that shows renderings of the entire 3.9 mile planned light rail line between SoDo and Alaska Junction. Set to open by 2035 , the 3 Line is the next light rail project planned for construction in the wake of a feverish pace of grand openings over the past two years.

The new images, which reflect the project's design as of this past July, provide an illustration of the significant amount of value engineering that Sound Transit conducted on the line – work that likely saved the project from the chopping block this past spring as the agency grappled with a major budget gap.

From a slimmed-down SoDo station – which will be the northern terminus of the line until the Ballard Link project opens as early as 2042 (or as late as 2060) – to a more compact Alaska Junction, Sound Transit was able to drive down the cost of the line by more than $2 billion between 2024 and 2026.

That work to cut costs has come with real trade-offs for riders. The video shows the new plan for the 3 Line to enter a tunnel near Nucor Steel's West Seattle plant at SW Yancy Street, bypassing a planned station under Avalon Way SW that would have served a growing section of the neighborhood. Without that station, Sound Transit was able to redesign the location of the planned guideway and tunnel portal to avoid having to displace several high profile properties, including a portion of the West Seattle Health Club.

But in contrast with the infill station that opened in North Seattle late last month, it will not be possible to come back later and build Avalon Station down the road if Sound Transit's finances somehow turn around, or voters approve a Sound Transit 4.

On August 13, Sound Transit and the City of Seattle announced another major design refinement for West Seattle Link, one that would be hard to notice in a flyover rendering. A major transmission line that is currently located next to the dedicated busway through SoDo will be relocated closer to the planned light rail guideway, avoiding major disruptions on a nearby street.

"The new SODO segment design will relocate major City infrastructure, Seattle City Light’s 230 kilovolt and 26 kilovolt transmission poles and lines, entirely within the light rail project footprint in the SODO Busway," a City announcement noted at the time. "This means that Sound Transit will not need to move massive powerlines onto 6th Ave S, which significantly reduces construction and lasting impacts on adjacent properties and businesses. The new design is expected to save the project over $100 million and remove the risk of damage to other critical City transportation and water infrastructure."

Since the May 28 board vote that rebalanced the larger Sound Transit 3 (ST3) plan and kept West Seattle Link on track, Sound Transit officials have been touting how swiftly the agency has been moving and heading toward construction. In August, the board unlocked an additional $765 million in budget authorization, setting up a construction support services contract that includes preparations for the Duwamish River crossing.

Just last week, the board's system expansion committee approved another set of property acquisitions, including the West Seattle Corporate Center (the former Bartell Drugs corporate headquarters), which will become a major truck staging point for tunneling work to Alaska Junction. If approved by the full board later this month, that will mark the fifth set of property acquisition approvals that the agency has received, getting the agency's real estate team to work.

This week's flyover video makes work that is often happening behind the scenes more tangible for future riders, even if an opening date nine years in the future seems incredibly distant. Once the 3 Line is fully connected with the rest of the light rail network with the opening of Ballard Link, travelers getting from Westlake Station to Alaska Junction will see their travel times cut by 50%, a major upgrade from current C Line service. But there's a lot standing in the way of that benefit becoming reality.
For now, transit fans will have to live vicariously through YouTube.

articles.title: Duplicative services and commuter route truncation, again
articles.author: Sherwin Lee
paras: We’re about a month into the Fall shakeup, where a substantial number of service changes were implemented to improve connections to Link. This is a recurring playbook that Metro has used ever since light rail service began: identify duplicative services and restructure existing bus routes to connect to Link stations rather than running all the way into downtown Seattle.

When Northgate Link opened, Sound Transit truncated many of its 510 series routes to connect at Link instead. After Lynnwood Link, all of Community Transit’s direct services to downtown Seattle were restructured . And with the August changes , both Metro and Sound Transit no longer offer any one-seat rides from Bellevue or Issaquah to Seattle, save for the 2 Line.

Critics of this approach generally lament the loss of the one-seat ride, that trip times generally increase when factoring in wait times, and that Link is not necessarily faster point-to-point than express routes. The Sound Transit subreddit and other various community forums feature countless examples of riders testifying to that end. There is even now a “Restore 554” petition circulating among Issaquah residents, urging the restoration of a direct Issaquah-Seattle route.

The planning justifications for this type of restructuring are quite straightforward: Link provides a frequent high-capacity serve to major regional centers; instead of running costly peak-directional bus service, reinvest the hours into boosting local connecting service. This implementation aligns with Jarrett Walker’s “frequency is freedom” mantra and is generally a position this blog has supported.

In practice, however, real-world conditions can muddy the picture. Take, for example, the 554’s successor: the 556, which now provides frequent all-day service between Issaquah and Bellevue. Those previously using the 554 (or the 550 local stops along Bellevue Way) to get to Seattle must now connect at South Bellevue Station for the same trip.

These transfer conditions can greatly deteriorate due to local northbound congestion on Bellevue Way just in the short span between the I-90 off-ramp and the station bus stops. Riders agonizingly wait for traffic to crawl up Bellevue Way only to see Seattle-bound trains glide past over their heads. Even in the southbound direction, buses have to yield to northbound traffic in order to turn into the station bays, which adds travel time variability.
The physical infrastructure in between the connecting services is important too. Jarrett Walker touches on this point in one of his foundational articles on transferring:

… the unpleasantness of the connection experience depends on many details of how the connection works. If two buses or trains arrive on opposite sides of a platform, facing one another five meters apart, with their doors open at the same time, walking out of one and into the other is a pretty low level of inconvenience for most passengers. If the connection involves getting off a bus, crossing a busy street, and waiting for another bus not knowing when it will arrive, the inconvenience is much greater.

As it were, the connecting infrastructure at South Bellevue and Mercer Island stations is less than ideal. Both settings require a moderate walk (across a signalized intersection in the latter case, largely thanks to Mercer Island’s opposition to an 80th Ave transfer point) and ascending or descending to the train platform. This can add a lot of variability, particularly for those with limited mobility, on top of the wait for the connecting service.

Negative feedback is often amplified over positive feedback, as human beings are far more likely to complain about things that hurt them rather than praise the things that help them. But in many ways, what is often seen as a degradation in one part of the network typically means an improvement in another part.

554 riders, for example, might glowingly reminisce about the quick travel times across I-90, but forget about the frequent outbound reliability issues inflicted by 2nd Avenue congestion (as I so often personally experienced). And although not quite a zero sum game, the changes have meant a substantially better commute for Issaquah-Bellevue riders, among other parts of the system.

Big restructures in the regional network will invariably result in system-wide tradeoffs, but that doesn’t mean agencies’ hands are tied. Barring a miraculous way of sending buses congestion-free right up (or down) to the Link platforms, transfer penalties can be offset by improving frequency and reliability across all segments.

Making the 556 a frequent all-day route that connects to frequent 2 Line service is certainly an excellent start, but continued work on reliability improvements are always in order. This might mean more attentive maintenance to ensure fewer breakdowns of Link trains. Or it could mean stronger partnerships with WSDOT and local jurisdictions to give signal or lane priority to buses.

Whatever the solution, transit agencies cannot go it alone here. Route 8’s dramatic reliability leaps were only possible by some repainting (and other minor infrastructural improvements) from SDOT. In the same way, local jurisdictions owe it to the taxpaying public to squeeze out the full return on our massive regional investment in transit. Helping create reliable well-connected services is a small, but important step to get there.

articles.title: Ballard Link Community Forum on October 19
articles.author: Nathan Dickey
paras: Seattle City Councilmember (District 6) and Sound Transit Boardmember Dan Strauss is hosting a community form discussing the Ballard Link Extension alongside several other elected officials and Sound Transit representatives. The forum will be held in the Osberg Great Hall at the National Nordic Museum on Monday, October 19, from 6-8pm .

In a newsletter emailed to constituents last week, Dan Strauss announced the event while highlighting his efforts to get Sound Transit to commit to building the full Ballard Link Extension to Market Street. These included requiring Sound Transit staff to determine when the agency would be able to complete the Ballard Link Extension under current conditions, and looking for ways to reduce project costs in order to open the extension sooner. Currently, the agency expects to open the SODO to Seattle Center portion of the Ballard Link Extension in 2042.

In July, Sound Transit fulfilled Strauss’ first requirement with the announcement the rest of the project could be delayed to 2060 unless significant cost savings are found. When voters passed ST3 in 2016, the entire Ballard Link Extension was expected to open in 2035. In 2021, this schedule slipped to 2037 or 2039 as Sound Transit realized the cost to build a second Link-only tunnel under downtown and managing other complications would far exceed expectations . After calculating “bottom-up” cost estimates for the proposed design of the extension last year, the agency found the full project could cost nearly twice its previous estimate. Compounded with exploding cost estimates across ST3, the Sound Transit Board voted to defer construction of line past Seattle Center until costs were reduced or additional revenue were found.

Sound Transit says it may be able to open the full extension in 2042 if the agency can reduce the total estimated cost by $1 billion (or identify that much in new revenue), begin acquiring property by 2030, finish design by 2032, and lock in funding to start construction by 2033. Regardless, Ballard Link advocates remain dedicated to pushing Sound Transit to return to the originally promised date of opening in 2035.

At the community forum, Sound Transit is expected to share more about its proposed timeline for the Ballard Link Extension, the work agency staff have been doing to reduce costs, and its next steps for the project. There will also be a Q&A session.

Those interested in a seat should probably arrive early. The National Nordic Museum is located at the intersection of 28th Ave NW and NW Market Street, just under a mile west of the planned terminus of the Ballard Link Extension. Nearby bus stops are served by King County Metro Routes 17 and 44 .

articles.title: Cafe Lolo Is the Neighborhood Restaurant Every Neighborhood Deserves
articles.author: <name>Kat Thompson</name>
paras: If I were to describe the perfect neighborhood restaurant, Cafe Lolo would completely fit my definition. The food is comforting and nourishing, emphasizing local ingredients, which playfully come together in a way that feels both fresh and familiar. The space is draped in natural light that’s assisted by over a dozen lamps. The inviting dining room is covered in quirky Renaissance-inspired murals that don’t feel disruptive. There are to-go meal kits available for purchase, as well as local beers. It’s an atmosphere that invites you to unwind with a bottle of wine. Owners Leah Engel, Alex Halmi, and Brett Bankson are present, not only flitting about the room, but also cooking the dishes in the kitchen and laughing with customers. If I lived in the neighborhood, just off the main drag of Capitol Hill, it’s somewhere I’d want to return to over and over again.

Cafe Lolo has an extensive wine menu and many local beers, as well as bottles in the fridge you can pick up to-go. Although yes, the wine list — which includes just one glass from Washington, and more options from Oregon and Europe) — is worth perusing, the nonalcoholic tisanes are also made from seasonal ingredients. The strawberry rhubarb soda I had on my visit was effervescent and floral without an overpowering sweetness.

Like the rest of the menu, dessert will change pending seasons — but don’t skip it. My visit included a celebration of ripe, macerated strawberries over a semolina olive oil cake, which had a buttery crust and a tender interior crumb. There was also a scoop of rhubarb sorbet; light, sweet, and sharp.
